Miss Aileen Riggin, of the Women's
Swimming Association, one of the
foremost women divers in the world,
stood trial yesterday afternoon at
Amateur Athletic Union headquarters
on charges of professionalism, and
after lengthy session was acquitted.


Following it's usual custom the regis
tration committee did not make public
the charges against the fifteen-year-
old aquatic star until after the trial.
and it is doubtful if Miss Riggin knew
why she was called before the tribunal
until she had taken her seat on the
witness stand.


However, as Miss Riggin had done
nothing to impair her standing as an
amateur she had little difficulty with
the American Athletic Union officials.
The trouble started when a certain
news association sent out articles
to Dive" These articles found their
way to American Athletic Union head
quarters and an investigation was
started.


1t developed that Miss Riggin knew
nothing whatever about the matter and
had had no conversation with any one
regarding the articles.


Miss Riggin, who finished fourth in
the long distance swim championship
of American last Saturday had simply
been imposed upon, the committee de-
cided, and under the circum stances
that august body very properly gave
her clean slate. Miss Rggin was a
member of the last American Olympic
team, has retained counsel and will
bring legal action for damages against
the news association which sent out
the articles under her name.

Traffic between the Eastern and

through the Panama Canal nearly
doubled during the last fiscal year,
according to "The Panama Canal
: Record" covering the twelve months
ending June so. In 1921 the total was
1,s72.3s8 cargo tons, compared with
1852 ,527 tons in 1922. These ship
ments were carried In 555 vessels,
against 322 in the year before.


Total trade through the Panama
Canal did not vary greatly in the two
years, aggregating 11,599,000 cargo
tons in 1921, and 10.884,0 tons in
1922, The number OF vessels was
1882 in 1921, compared with 2,T36 in
1922.


Cargo tonnage moving over the
United States coastwise route was
about equally divided between east
bound and westbound traffic. The lead
ing commodities carried in the Allan
tic to Pacific trade were iron and
steel, coal, sulphur and miscellaneous
manufactured articles of all kinds,
while the bulk of the shipments in
the opposite direction consisted of
lumber. canned goods, oil, metals and
fresh and dried fruits.


Second only to the coastwise business
in volume was the trade to and from
the Far East. Considering Atlantic to
Pacific cargoes alone, the tonnage over
this route exceeded the United States
scoastwise tonnage by approximately
100000 tons, and was more than five
sstimes as great as that over any of the
remaining great trade routes. Cargo
from the Far East to the United
States through the canal was less
in 1922 than in 1921. This one-sided
traffic was due to the fact that many
OF the outgoing vessels return by way
OF the Suez Canal, the 'round-the world
cruise giving a better opportunity to
pick up return cargo than the trip
across the Pacific. The outgoing ship
N nents over this route consist mainly of
oils, iron and steel, railroad material,
machinery, raw cotton and. ammonia; !;
while in return the Far East sends
sugar, rice, tea, rubber, wool, cocoanut
and vegetable oils.


The third most important route
through the canal in point of cargo
tonnage was that between European
ports and the west coast Of the United
States. This also was a one-sided trade
route, with the bulk of the traffic
moving from the Pac fc to the Atlantic.

step toward uniting the regular army,
National Guard and reserves into zone
homogeneous citizen army Of the

standing features of the training

level Of accomplishment. Regulars,

worked side by side with growing

eleme in the national defense, and
Of the role each is to play. Conse-
quently, the work of this summer is
believed to constitute a long step for
ward toward uniting the several ele-
ments into one homogeneous citizen
army Of the United States"


5000 Reserves Participate

ganized reserves, the greater part Of
whom were commissioned officers dur"
ing the World War, participated in
field training for the first time this
year. "These reserve officers gen.
orally" Mr.. Weeks said, Cleft camp
with the strong feeling that their
period therein had been distinctly
profitable, and that the reserve or
longer could be justly called paper
army, but that in reality they repre-
sented most powerful element in the
real military strength of the nation"

soldiers participated in citizens mill
tary training camps this summer than
in 1921. obstruction in ALL" Secre-
tary Weeks said, "was SO organized as
to get the greatest possible esults with

energy, to the end that the government

the betterment of it's young man power

Postal receipts all over the country
indicate that business continues on
the up grade. The monthly reports
of the Post Office Department on the
amount of post Office business in the
fifty leading cities of the country
have shown steady climb since last
November. Last month, for the first
time, the Department compiled list
of the postal receipts in fifty selected
industrial cities considered as rep
resentatiye centers in their respec-
tive sections of the country. These
figures also support the belief that
business is mending.


Last month the fifty leading cities
in the country did post Office bust
ness amounting to $19.543,152, which
was an increase OF $2,034 410 over
July, 1921. The fifty selected cities
did a business amounting to $2,164,-
AL, an increase of $204 ,S94 over the
previous year. The gain, figured by
percentage, was almost as great in
the smaller cities, for the leading
fifty's gain was 1852 per cent. and
that OF the selected group was 10.45
per cent.


OF the fifty larger cities only two.
Rochester and Washington, reported
decreases for July. In the smaller
group nine showed decreases. These
were Norfolk, Virginia; Springfield,
Illinois; Wilmington, Delaware;
Schenectady, New York; Lynn, Mas
sachusetts; Columbia, South Car
olina; Manchester. New Hampshire;
Cumberland, Maryland; and Chey-
enne, Wyoming.


Fort Worth, Texas, reported gain
of $500 per cent. Other large cities
which made big gains were Akron,
Los Angeles, Cleveland, Springfield,
Massachusetts, and Columbus, Ohio,
all of which reported increases Of
more than 90 per cent. Albuquerque,
New Mexico, showed the biggest gain
of any city in the smaller group,
with an increase of 40.59 per cent.


Postal receipts are pretty nearly an
infallible index to the temper OF
business conditions. These figures
indicate restored confidence and
steadily strengthening activity.

The Cunarder Pannonia, recently
banished to the cargo carrying service
arrived last evening from London after
the most tumultuous and longest trip
OF her career. and came up to her
hudson River pier with a tug acting as
her rudder, her own having been smashed
In one OF the many hurricane tempests
that Kept her staggering twenty-nine
days through fierce seas.


From January % the liner was steerei
entirely by her twin screws. after her
skipper. Capt. Grunow, war veteran
had made several hazardous attempts
to repair the rudder. in which the lives
of volunteers were in peril.


The mightiest winds and waves came
in midocean on January %, when the
barometer fell to 27.S0. The Pannonia
kept her Prov to the upheaval and
vainly used oil to smooth the crests
that occasionally curled aboard. The
skipper used the old time term 'moun-
famous" to describe the great gray
backs" When the storm subsded a
bit 1t was found that the ship would
not answer her helm. An officer was
lowered over the stern and reported
that the rudder post had broken off at
the twenty-five foot draft mark and
a six foot section of the rudder blade
had been carried away.


The liner proceeded slowly, steering
with her twin screws, until the seas were
less wild, four days later. when Capt.
Grunovr ordered the after ballast tanks
emptied and the forward ones filled to
bring the stern up so that as much as
possible of the undamaged part OF the
rudder might be brought out OF the
water. Chief officer Eric Rees and First
Officer Thomas Mitchell went over the
stern in bo's'ns chairs and after an
hours hard work they made az inch
wire hawser fast to the swaying rudder.


The officers were being hauled aboard
when big sea slapped under the stern
tore away the hawser. ripping II TO
pieces and letting the rudder thrash
madly. Mitchell was knocked ~uncon-
scious The ship continued on her
stormy course. steering with her pro-
pelers.


A final effort to repair the rudder was
made on Thursday. 200 miles southeast
of Ambrose Channel .Lightship. First
officer Mitchell and Bo's'n Charles
ingram. each strapped to a bo'sn's
chair, made the wire hawser fast. but
vicious wave sent everything awry
again and Capt Grunow decided to make
port steering by the twin screws. He
called for help by wireless and the Mer-
rift & Chapman wrecking tug Resolute
was sent out to the Ambrose Channel
Lightship and came in as the liners
rudder, twin screws not being safe 70
guide a liner in inland waters.

picked up the crying triplets, and
softly wiped their tear.stained
cheeks; and. tying on some biblets,
they fed 'em Jam and bread and
milk: and then, q shining cloud,
they bore 'em off to dreamland to
forget the tumult loud. A million

time in speaking until they reach
ed the presence of the busy Bubble

Changed BY Electricity.


Look! Look! It's an electricl
When they paused beside the door

more bright brother Bubblejoys q
bursting from each washers frothy
top. and SO straightway they knew
they'd found Bubblejoyous shop
Now swift they roll that treasure
on its sturdy flying casters into
the kitchen that had been the
scene Of such disasters; then turn
a switch: soon soggy clothes
through wringer-rolls are spillinG
into that blessed washer with q
speed that's simply thrilling. Next
they add water hot: some soap
then start the whole thing spin
ming; and while those, saucy Bub.
blejoys roll round the kitchen grin
ming. fixing up soap and starch-
behold! the voices. rough and rasp
ing, stop grumbling. and their own
ers gather round the washer
sasping! They see how clean the
clothes turn tout; they watch how
In "a fifty, the BubbleJoys have
wrung 'em out, and rinsed 'etn,
sweet and spifty; they marvel
while soiled sock and shirt, pink
silk and bright.hued gingham c0me
magic-clean: they marvel more to
see the wringer wiring 'em.


Now. when the frantic husband
saw the Bubblejoys a-saving his
homes tranquility; how. they had
come and stopped the awful ravinR
Of kinfolk who'd lambasted him taz
though his wife he'd beaten) he
vowed he'd buy a wash.machine
before he'd slept or eaten.


He did. And then the Bubble
joys took off their aprons friliy
and put 'em in their pockets; and,
with giggles sweet and silly. they
floated back to help their Queen
mix gorgeous-tinted starch and
stretch her robes against the
sky-a bright effulgent arch.

MO longer will the flapper flap

Demurely downward stray.

They used to say, not long ago,
II women had the vote,

well sweep the universe!'

communists and fascist continued
throughout the labryinth Of Genoa's
narrow winding streets. The capture

flags and other socialist trophies by

Fascist and communists occurred in
the Via Canonia, Milan. when the
Fascist invaded and wrecked COM
munist club. Two were killed and
many on both sides were wounded.
The fascist had evacuated the mum
icipal building at Milan and all were
hoping peace would soon return,
when from a window in the building
Of the socialist newspaper Avanti
gestures of scorn and mockery were
made to the fascist. The latter.
thereupon, furiously attacked the
building, which they entered and
partly wrecked. They were finally
elected by royal guards. The number
Of casualties is not known.

Again the men Of the District fire
department have met the test. Wash
ington always has had supreme faith
in her firefighters. In the past they
have proved their efficiency and hero
ism many times.


But perhaps never have these quail
ties been more strikingly shown than
during the gigantic efforts put forth
by the score and more fire companies
which attended the Knickerbocker
Theater disaster.


First upon the scene, the firemen
lost no time in turning themselves
from firehghters into rescuers, men
Of mercy, using their training as fire.
men to fight disheartening mass Of
steel which was crushing the lives out
Of hundreds.


All that terrible night and all day
Sunday the firemen were there, hack
ing, saving, pulling out the wounded
and tenderly bearing away the dead.
Without their skilled help. their acute
understanding Of just what to do and
how to do it, the toll Of the catas-
trophe would be higher today.


During the same eventful night
many fires broke out over the city.
and other companies responded, con-
tending with well-nigh impossible
snow. But they got to their fires.
They put the fires out.


Chief Watson and all his men en-
gagged, all the men Of the department,
in fact, are to be congratulated. They
have the grateful thanks of the city.
and. best Of all, the satisfaction of
knowing that in the hour Of need they
were strong.

CAPE MAY, n. j.. Sept 1O-Max Bel
berback, the son of Philadelphia den-
tist, entertained crowd of his friends
on the beach at Cape May Point here
this afternoon by throwing sticks into
Delaware Bay for his dog, water
spaniel. to fetch. He threw them fur
Their and further. and each time the
dog swan out battled with the fast
flowing ebb tide and brought them safe
~ to shore. where ne laid them at his
masters feet and wagged his tail in the
consciousness of difficult job we'll done.


But finally young Beiberback threw
the stick too far. so far that it could
barely be seen bobbing about on the
waves. But the dog leaped into the
water and started swimming toward it.
He kept on, even though BeiberbaclS
tried to whistle him back. fearing that
the tide would catch the dog and pre-
vent him swimming back. But the dog
reached the stick, and then tried to re-
turn to the beach. the stick cutched
firmly between his teeth.


1t was apparent at once that the dog
could not make it. He was not strong
enough to battle against the swift tide
and the big rollers that by this time
had begun to comb the beach. He
could be seen every few minutes, top
ping a big wave and swimming furi-
ously. and still with the stick held in
his mouth.


Young Beiberback plunged into the
bay without even stopping to remove
his clothing. He had hard fight to
reach the dog, and when he did he had
harder fight to bring the animal back
to the beach. The tide got them both
In its grip and swept them into the
rips where the bay and the ocean meet,
and had not young Beiberback been an
exceptionally strong swimmer both
he and the dog would have been
drowned. The spaniel seemed to know
that his master was trying to help him,
for from time to time they topped wave
and the people on the shore could see
the little dog lying quietly in young
Beiberback's arms--and still with the
stick clutched in his mouth. Beiber-
back said afterward that the dog would
not relinguish the stick, even though he
ordered him to.


The young man and the dog battled
with the waves and the tide for half
an hour. drawing nearer and nearer the
beach. and finally they got to point
where they could make more Roadway.
BY this time the dog was rested, and
Beiberback let the animal slip from
his arms. Then the dog and his master
swan to the beach side by side, and
when they had crawled exhaused onto
the sand the dog crept forward, laid the
stick at young Beiberback's feet and
wagged his tail as heartily and as en-
thusia stically as he could. for he was
painting and shivering and was half
drowned

and horror Of the ruined Knicker-

dead or injured, and as the full weight
OF the losses became known the dead
monopolized the space. crowding tie
injured in the all too small rooms.


1t was merely a first aid station
Tor those taken crushed, but alive,
from the wreckage. They were car
ried in stretchers over the slippery
pavement with lines of soldiers keep
ing the crowds far back Surgeons
and nurses and women eager to bring
their sympathy and cheer to the suf-

under debris until the rescuers cut
the victim loose. Bandages were ap-
piled and then the injured were taken
away to hospital or home.


AisIes of the Dead.


But the dead lay along in the double
rows in wh:.... :hey stretched across the
floor, lay until fearful relative or
friend, a husband or wife or father or
nother recognized the crused form

The dead walked those whose fears had
drawn them here because of some one

sleepers made the journey of sorrow

leaned to draw back the coverings, and
then gasp with short lived relief as

Some OF these seekers came with the

mass. They had worked hours with
the rescuers to find that one, only to
turn now and then for hurried trip

Eleven times death struck down hus-

The times when children were taken

ater has been in its earlier hours of a

ccaslng activity. The losers In the

timony of the first who reached the the
ater that the outcry there in the FUN

The trades union of England. current

unions apparently are the most affected.

for instance. has declined 100000, that
of the general workers $4,000 and the
railwaymen's union 1000.


VIII Thorne. NJ p. secretary Of the
National Union of General Workers,
says the assets of that union fell during
last year from $751; ,673 to f272.452, due

ing after the war, a general slackening
In trade. the payment of unemployment

come impossible for any politician even 70

! recent gathering was called at Chatta-

GENEVA, Sept. 1.-THE Council of
the League of Nations to-day declined
any direct intervention in Greco-Turk
affairs and notified the Kemalist au-
thorlties that their note addressed to
the league on the subject of atrocities
alleged to have been committed bv the
Greeks had been transmitted to the
various governments represented in the
Council.


Both the Turks and the Councils
correspondence was forwarded through
the medium of the international com
mittee of the Red Gross.


The council passed on its opinion
that, assuming the Turks charges are
true, the kemalists are not obliged on
their part to break the rules of civil
lied warfare. Such mild advice, it was
agreed here to-day, was not likely to
prevent the Turks from taking ter
rlbie revenge on the Greeks remain
ing in Asia Minor and the govern
ments represented in the league coun-
csl were powerless to prevent this,
whereas the supreme council could
frame reply exerting considerable
moral pressure on the Kemalists.


The Earl of Balfour. British repre-
sentative on the supreme council, in
brief statement tonight said that
the Greco Turkish situation was one
the governments could regulate. but
not the league. He did not comment
on the fact that the governments.
chiefly England and France, had per
sistentiy failed for many months to
bring. about peace in the Near East
and that the present situation was the
result.

LONDON, December 16.-There is
a music boom on in England at the
present time and the musicians and
the music industry are enjoying n
period of great prosperity. notwith-
standing the general trade depres-
sion. The reason for this is the great
interest in musical entertainments
for the public and the popularity of
dancing.


Musicians have suffered little from
unemployment during the dark days
in other trades and businesses. Out
of the 5000 musicians who specialize
in theater. music hall and cinema or
chestras there are barely 100 without
work.


The fact that there is dancing prac-
tically everywhere creates keen de-
mand for instrumentaliSts, many of
whom earn more than two guineas
nightly.


Choral societies have been revived
since the war and this year many
new ones have been started through
out the country. creating an increas-
ed demand for solo vocaNsts, orches-
tras and sheet music. The piano.
building trade also has experienced a
boom. Most of the factories have
been working overtime, for months.
This is due partly to the increased
call for pianos at home and abroad
and the fact that trade in German
made instruments has virtually been
killed.

CHICAGO, July 26.-The
cunning little flapper, with her
bobbed hair, skirts that are
little more than a girdle, rolled
socks and cigarettes, must mend
her ways. Long skirts with
waists that come up fairly close
around the throat are coming
back, and Miss Flapper will
have to renovate her methods,
for late hours, roll-your-owns,
and all that do not go with
long skirts.

Eastern representatives Of the
Women's Apparel Association,
which began its convention here
today. Flapperish ways, these
delegates say, will not do with
the new styles. They admit
the sprightly young things will
feel awkyard for awhile in
long gowns, but they must get
used to them.


Along with the new styles,
which leave something to the
imagination, will come an end
to the bobbed-hair craze. Arti-
fetal curls and other trickery
will be resorted to in order to
make the hair comport with
the long skirts.

| ing"

BosToN, Aug. 29.-Americans stand
triumphant to-day in the first tennis
test with the Australian challengers.
Before a gallery that jammed and
overflowed the spacious Longwood
stands William T. Tilden and Vincent
Richards. playing in defense OF their
national doubles championship title,

overwhelmed them. in fact. after a
nervous uncertain start.

ard outscored the Americans in spec
tacular battle of tennis Titans. and then
their formidability waned as Tilden and
Richards. with ever increasing power
and with delightful daring struck their
best stride. individually and concertedly,
and turned the tide The contest went
four sets, 4--6, 6-1. 6-3, Cd.


1t was decisive victory for the cham
ptons. decisive, clear cut and impressive,
and now there Is little doubt that it will
be Tilden and Richards in the doubles





Forest Hills next Saturday. incidentally
it was the third national doubles title
for the top ranking pair and title never
more convincingly earned.

who pointed out that the Australians
probably were not as keen to win the
national title as they will be in their
fight for the international title in the
Davis cub series to come: that during
the four days of vain waiting for the
weather to clear and permit the COM
pletion of the event they had even of
fered to default the final SO as. to reach
the scene of the Davis cup event.


From first to last In to-day's play the
spectacular versatility of Tiden. his
infinite stroke variety, his tremendous
service, his strategy and sharp angled
finishing shots stood out with glaring
prominence. Richards with his fine vol
leying and smashing and skillful placing
proved an able assistant after he had
recovered from an erratic streak that
clung to him for all of one set.


On the other side of the net O'Hara
Wood easily outshone his partner. He
was the better strategist, the more
subtle in his sharp angled placements
and his change of pace, and 1t was his
SPARKLING play that earned the first set
a. time when the champions were not
yet in stride Patterson was prone to
net and drive out of court at critical
stages His first service was not under
control and his second service ball was
handled more easily than he had antici-
pated His overhead smashing, too,
lacked severity and finality. The court
after three days rain was not nearly as
fast as he prefers il and the big Aus
ftralian did not cover court with his GUS
tomary boldness and agility.

concentrate particularly on Patterson
backhand. as many had expected them
TO, still Patterson clearly indicated that

running around the ball and taking 1t

portunity.

cally. Only OHara Wood of the four
players seemed to get into stride with

followed in the matter of attaining top
speed The rallies were fairly evenly
fought at that stage, and the set de-
veloped only one break through service.
through Richards's service in the sew

The Sicilian bandit is no invention of
the storybook. as the weary police who
have just captured the notorious brigand
Andaloro can testify. Using the tactics
of the Malta and the Camorra. for six
years Andaloro ranged the island rob-
bing, numbering and terrorizing the citi-
Zens to such an extent that they dared
not bulge from their houses when they
knew he was in the province.


Andaloro killed several police officials
and private enemies, but his worst crime
was the murder of nine members OF n
family with whom he had lived, lnclud-
ing three women. The police issued
thirty warrants for his arrest. but no.
body had the temerity TO attempt the
capture of the blackbearded brigand.
Finally, under pressure by terrorized
Sicilans. the police organized an elabo-
rate hunt, tightening the circle around
Andaloro till he was traced TO a cave
near the sea-


He had blocked the entrance. but the
police used pickaxes TO good effect.
Then none dared enter the cavern where
Andalero waited. The police forced an
associate OF Andaloro'S to enter. but her
fear Of the brigand was greater than
her fear OF the police. and she ran
out shriekng. Finally two lieutenants
braved the dark recesses and dragged
out the Blackhander.


Now the police are catching their
breath before making an effort to cap
ture Andaloros band and dozens OF
other outlaws who pursue their preda-
tory careers on the island.

CHICAGO, Feb. 24.--Railway express

decision to-day. eliminating time and
one-half pay for the ninth hour and
creating split trick" of eight hours

time rates.

agreement made under Federal control
with the American Railway Express
Company. They will cover about $4,000
employees, several thousand shop men
having been included in rules negotiated
by the company and the federated shop
crafts last year.

rules retain in principle eight hours as
constituting a days work. Time and
one-half will be paid for all work over
nine hours. Time and one-half was for
merly paid after eight hours.


In the split trick arrangement eight
hours work may be spread over twelve
hours, where relief is provided of one
hour or more at a time. This change
permits men to work when needed most.



penalizing the express company for
overtime. Split tricks were authorized
under the old agreement when five or
more men were employed, but the new
rules are effective regardless of the
number employed.


Sunday and holiday work will be paid
for at the pro rata rate as in the past.


For employees paid by the month, $40
hours shall constitute a month, but
overtime will not be paid until after go
hours. Formerly time and one-half
was paid after 240 hours.


The board set rate of 50 cents an
hour for men employed in train service
but not regularly assigned. Helpers
will receive so cents both with mini
mum guarantee of eight hours.

employees

BERLIN, Sept. 17.-The uncertain
political situation and money famine
continued to dominate the situation
during the last week, although toward
the end there arose a distinct optimism
regarding an ultimate understanding
between Belgium and Germany which
was reflected in recovery of the
mark, closing the week with 1880 to

negotiations of President Havenstein,
of the Reichsbank, with London, par
ticularly his conversations with Lloyd
George. Should the British banks be
willing to guarantee part Of Germany's
obligations to Belgium for the rest of
marks, there is every indication of
Germany getting some respite, however
short, during which more thorough
adjustment of the reparations problem
may be hoped for.


The money shortage situation on the
other hand shows little hope of early
improvement. For the first time the
Reichsbank wass actually compelled to
close it's doors one day this week, while
banks throughout the country exhibited
signs "No Payment Made" This situa-
tion was caused by the Reichsbank
being called upon to ship two billion
marks to Upper Silesia, where workers
had been growing dangerously restive
because employers were unable to
meet payrols. Rumblings of indus
trial trouble came during the week
from the Rhine and Ruhr sections,
where railroad men were reported pre-
pairing wage demands as a result of
intensive communist agitation.

week the cost of living registered sew
eral new high points, emphasizing
again grave prospects for the coming
winter. During August the cost of

In the last three years the Long

roadbed and tracks in good repair

made, and unsafe rails detected and
removed.

manual, have been operated at some.
thing nearly approaching 100 per

'twenty-four- hour day" and the

ernment, have not drawn any
salaries for months.

per cent.

shutdown. All the mills were closed
today. for they have not operated on
Saturday since the four-day schedule

the opportunity to address the opera
tives at two large mass meetings.

hall this afternoon under the auspices

other meeting. called by the United
Textile Workers of America, was
scheduled for tonight.

tie the coal strike is called to order
here Monday. This became apparent
to-day when operators with headquar-
tors in Cleveland prepared to resist
the United Mine Workers demands for
a renewal of the old wage scale.

with the non-union operators of Penn
syvania and West Virginia, they de-
clared to-day. The inside day labor
rate under the old scale was $3.50,
and cutters pay was proportionately
higher.

burgh Vein Operators Association,

to-day that when the conference is
held there will be found within the
miners union representation strong
element favoring a lower wage scale
for competitive purposes with the non
union fields.

Loie Fuller emerged last evening from
her partial seclusion to give Paris an
entertainment in the form of dances by
her pupils which the critics are praising

TWO young Englishmen have been rescued
after spending twelve months marooned on
the Antarctic continent. Left behind when an
exploring expedition sailed away to Montevideo,
they found themselves buried alive in an endless
expanse of ice.


Robinson Crusoe's adventures were common
place compared with the experiences through which
But as indication of the adaptability Of human
beings they survived. somewhat enjoyed the life,
and we're fat and healthy when rescued.


The annals of the Antarctic contain
thrilling episodes than those related by T. Bag
Shave. Cambridge University student, when he
returned in London the other day. First, the two
constructed hut from the wreckage of their
boat Despite the intense cold of the long polar
winter they made themselves comparatively COM
Portable From bits of driftwood and stones they
fashioned furniture and table implements.


Their food throughout the year consisted
largely of polar fish, seal meat and penguin eggs.
Neither had single sick day.


All this is evidence that the human race is
growing stronger and more adaptable physically.
Explorers of fifty years ago. it is probable, would
have pershed after single month OF the life these
men were forced to lead. But men arriving
rapidly at the point where physical inconvenience
mean little.


They found life in the home of eternal winter
rather interesting after they became accustomed 10
it, OF course, there human habitations,
but the two found enjoyable companionship in
the penguin flocks These birds they describe as
having much the same kind of family life as human
beings, with marriage divorce ETC.


Doubtless they brought back from the Antarc-
tic continent some valuable scientific data. Every
day they took atmospheric observations, records OF
which they preserved carefully until their rescuers
arrived. But statistics Of such kind do not inter-
est the general public.


In the story of their adventures, however, they
brought back something which should exist as long
stories of polar exploration recounted in the
English language. They have invested the Antarc-
tic continent that great white waste of mystery,
with human interest. They have demonstrated the
ability of men to live under such conditions Prob
ably they are the first white men ever to spend
winter in quite the same situation. Their expert
ences should prove valuable to future explorers.

Special Dispatch TO The Star.


KANSAS CITY. July 27.-The delay
in the threshing of wheat caused by
wet weather throughout the south
west has been more than offset by the
benefit to corn and pasturage. Crop
conditions. usually the outstanding
influence at this season here. continue
encouraging. but the depressing in
fluence of the coal and rail strikes
continues to grow, although the slow
ing down OF business has been more
the result of fear for the future than
any immediate transportation or fuel
shortage.


The significant development of the
business situation has been the small
ness of the demand for funds to
finance the wheat harvest. With the
harvest over in Kansas, the nations
greatest wheat state. bank deposits
are greater than they were when the
harvest began. The bankers see in
this fact the development of more
efficiency and economy on the farms
and draw the conclusion that the
wheat crop will mean more than in
other years in purchasing power.


Wholesale and retail trade in dry
goods and kindred lines has declined
moderately, but IL the strike situation
clears. the outlook for the remainder
of the year is hopeful. Special end
of-the-season sales are stimulating
retail trade materially just now.

Sir: About forty-six Assyrian
Christians from Persia have arrived

annual quota, which is eighty, was ex-

citizenship papers; they are we'll es-

ers. stockmen, business men and
bankers-men who are in position to
know the trend of conditions-and

Discouragement and despair have
given away to confidence and hope.
Tho decentralization that existed six
months ago has been overcome, and
they are going ahead with courage

pletely out of the woods, but broader
markets and the increased values Of
agricultural commodities enable them

This day finds us at the culmina-
tion Of American sport. At New
Haven $4,000 persons win see the
forty-first football meeting Of Har-
ward and Yale in series which has
become the most famous Of all>inter-
collegiate competitions. 1t is our
most brilliant sporting classic, and
this year 1t loses no luster from the
fact that both Of the rivals have al
ready been defeated by the astonish-
ing team from Princeton. At Phila-
delphia $4,000 enthusiasts will
gather while the Army and the Navy
have it out in the twenty-flfth game
of another football series which has
done much to spread the gospel Of
fair play, clean, hard competition
and true sportsmanship in this
country.


Football followers deplore the fact
that this year these two events con-
fiict. But in coming on the same
afternoon they produce day of days
which certainly has no parallel in
any other country and which has
been equaled here on only few oc-
casions. To the record breaking
crowds which will see the big con-
tests in the East add the overflow
ing stadiums and stands at the
Minnesota, Chicago Wis
consin and Iowa. Northwestern bat
ties in the Middle West and the Pa
cific coast classic which will bring
together California and Stanford
and you have striking testimonial
not only for football itself but for
the place sport occupies in this ma
tion Of ours.


For Yale football this is a day of
tremendous import. Not since 1916
have the Ellis defeated Harvard. Since
1907 they have crossed the Crimson's
goal line only once. To-day the Blue,
which was glorious and powerful in
defeat at Princeton last week, faces
a Harvard eleven which has been
downed twice in succession, by
Princeton and Brown.


Yale hopes run high and this may
be the Yale year for which the Bull
dog has been waiting anxiously many
seasons. However, for Harvard II
may be said that when It meets the
Blue all past performances count for
naught. 1t is game which has con-
founded experts only too often and
turned prophecies into fallacies.


AS for the Army and the Navy,
there's another fight which defles
prognostication. They have the
splendid spirit OF our national SER
vice, the tremendous enthusiasm of
youth and physical perfection. these
cadets and midshipmen. and they
never are beaten until the final
whistle blows.

Berlin, April IL.


Following a wild report that 800, ,000
Americans were planning to visit Ger
many this summer, the Germans imme-
diately began to make calculations in
higher mathematics how many rooms
and meals. three per day. and how many
extra railroad cars would be necessary
to transport the American invasion. The
hotels began to hoard foodstuffs, specu-
lators sought to corner stocks Of trinkets
and housewives who lid not see any
profits to be made from the tourists
feared they would be eaten out of house
and home.


There are some $4,000 registered for a
visit to Oberammergau. Cooks esti-
mates that $4,000 is the outside figure
for the numper of tourists who will cross
the Atlantic tn the available ship space
this summer. Shipping companies say
that all return cabin space on returning
ships has been filed for August and Sep
tember.


Hotels Double Prices.


Practically all first class hotels
charge double room prices to foreigners.
Some distinguish between foreigners
from countries with high and low cur
rencies. This is done in different ways.
Frankfort hotels give native guests re-
bate. Berlin hotels include a double
price on the bill. while some add q
supplementary bill.


The manager Of the Adion Hotel says
that Americans occupy so per cent. OF
his rooms and that he gives Americans
priority. He thinks the extra price for
foreigners is right because of their
ability TO pay more and because OF the
difficulty of asking old permanent Ger
man guests to vacate. He says he has
no reason for complaint. Indeed, the
Aldon receives daily from so to 100
more requests for rooms than it can
meet


The head of the official Berlin tourist
agency says that the upkeep of Berlin
hotels had risen considerably. especially
in those where the comforts which for
eign visitors demand arc supplied. He
thinks that the foreigners should bear
this extra burden. He says that there
is not sufficient room In Berlin hotels
for the tourists who already are flock
ing here. but that there are many good
second class hotels where luxuries are
missing but which ara clean and COM
Portable. In these prices are not half
as high as at the large hotels. the
average being so cents to 81 a day.


BfIIeting system introduced.


Berlin is organizing a hilieting system
along the lines which proved successful
at the Frankfort and Leipzig fairs.
Families with spare rooms are urged
to register at the central bureau. Here
rooms are classified according TO the
conveniences and comforts provided and
priced accordingly. Tourists coming TO
Berlin will find sandwich men indicating
where the rooming agencies are located.


Many Berliners hesitate to register
their rooms for fear compulsory room
ing commission might requisition their
extra rooms and All them with unde-
eirable guests The tourist agency pro-
poses to circumvent this by promising
professional secrecy. These rooms are
particularly recommended to Americans
with moderate means and all who have
not made advance reservations during
the rush season.


The Baltic watering places are en-
tirely rented out for the summer season,
mostly to Swedish visitors. who are
coming to enjoy the low exchange.

Sonneberg in Thuringia, Germanys

s:.-ugh trimmings were restrained. often

promising fulfillment of the expectation

brilliant in Ascot's history. But at noon

gayly colored parasols which offered

yellow.

colored waistcoats being notable. Lord
Londsdale-grand old man Of British
sport-was one Of the few wearing a
gray morning coat with gray topper.


While the rain marred the opening
day from the standpoint of FASHION,
racing was complete success from the
standpoint of racing men. The rockllKe
turf was softened by the rain.

leagues.

PARIS, May 3 (Associated Press) =
The Preparations Commission has noti-
fed the State Department at Washing
ton that it will terminate the delivery
of German dyes 20 the Textile Alliance
Of America on June 80. Unless the de-
partment officially designates the alli-
ance or some other American agency by
that time the commission will probably
appoint committee to select medium
through which the dyes can be sold in
America. This decision was taken after
the commission had waited nearly six
months for the United States Govern
ment to approve the alliances arrange
ment with the commission.


Officials of the alliance recently made
a new agreement with the German Dye
Alliance through which the American
textile industry was to receive largely
increased deliveries of dyes essential to
the successful development of the indus
try. The hope is expressed in commits
sion circles that this latest action will
move the United States Government to
act before June 80.

The battle in Kilkenny ended this
evening. At o'clock Ormonde Castle,
the last stronghold held by the irregV-
lars, was stormed and captured by the
Free State troops.


The irregular garrison surrendered
and was marched. with its arms and
ammunition. to the military barracks.
< At 10 o'clock this morning storming
parties under command Of Col. Prout
advanced, on the castle by different
routes, followed by an armored car.
They were fired upon by snipers In the
streets and a fierce engagement ensued.
The irregulars who yesterday were
driven from the Parliament street bar
racks formed the main part Of the
castles defenders.

BELFAST, May (Associated Press) -
A large number of armed men rushed
into the Royal Irish Constabulary bar
racks at Bellagaha, South Derry, and
fired several volleys at the occupants,
killing one constable and wounding Ser
geart Kerr. Two other constables also
were slightly wounded.


Barracks at Draperstown and Lesert-
martin. County Londonderry, also were
attacked.


An attempt to burn a weaving factory
at Limavady, also in Londonderry, was
frustrated by the watchman, who dis
covered that the doors had been sprin-
kled with petrol and found a can OF
petrol near by. The Ballykenny flax
mills, near Limavady. were burned.

Congress always has been a stick
Ter for system until the time came
around each year for making appro.

Nine hundred school children were

them and settled on the roofs Of
dozen and more houses.


Considering the danger they were

fire, there was very little panic among
the children. They were frightened.
of course. Some of them whimpered
and cried, and a few shrieked with
fear, but those that did were soon
Gained by the priest and the nun, who
went among the children telling calmly

only obey orders and march out as
they had done many times before in
their fire drills.

was 80 o'clock when the fire started,
and II was only few minutes later thai
every child was safely in the streets.
Once outside the children's relatives,
who had rushed In terror to the church
and the school when they heard that the
buildings were on fire, quickly drew
them away from the vicinity of the
aames. Embers and sparks and bits of
charred wood fell like wind about the
burning structure. or borne high on
northeasterly wind they rose and scared
to the roofs of other houses. But the
Passaic Fire Department did such good
work that only three other buildings
were burned besides the church and the
school although many others were
ignited.


The police OF Passaic said that the
fires started in the basement OF a sa-
loon at 2i Wall street. This building
was a three STORY frame structure, the
two upper floors being occupied by
families Before the firemen arrived
the two two-story buildings to the
south, IS and 30 Wall street, were

The church and school. which cost
$50, 900. was to the north of the burn
ing buildings. The cnurcfl caught fire
soon, but even before that the priest
and the un were going among the
children. getting them in line. encour-
aging them to sing and to be brave. so
that when the time came they went
quickly and solidly in line down the
stairs and out of doors.


The fire was visible to the men work.
ing in the woolen and other mills OF
Passaic. They threw down their tools

After a two weeks training cruise In
New England waters the Naval Re-
serves Of the Sixth Battalion on board
two Eagle boats, under Commander R.
J.. Wilson, returned yesterday after
noon to their base at the East Twenty
fourth Street pier. The fotilla, which
had lifted anchor at Vineyard Haven,
Mass, on Friday morning, was met
down the bay by Commander Charles
Boon, head Of the Sixth Battalion, who
boarded the vessels and inspected
them.


This was the second cruise of the
three which the Naval Reserves make
every summer to keep it's membrs fit
and ready for any emergency. On
board the two Eagle boats, Nos. 15 and
Do, vessels somewhat larger than a
submarine chaser and built during the
war, were thirty officers and 40 men.
The fotilla left New York on August
and made Its first stop at New Lon
don, Conn.,, where the presence Of sew
eral submarines gave the Eagle crew
an opportunity to study the actual
maneuvering Of Subs" under water.

ious drill practices and the training

For sixteen hours in the North Sea
Potomac battled desperately with a
fire that threatened their ship and
was not extinguished until Capt. Will
lam Macleod had tried trick learned
in war.


The liner, which arrived yesterday
at Hoboken with superstructure dam
aged by the confiagration, left Bremen
on the afternoon of March 2. About
eight hours later a fire was discov-
cred in hatch No. 4. next to the fire
room. 1t was brisk and rapidly grow
ing, feeding from straw mattresses
and ships stores.


With steam and with hose lines the
ships crew fought. The chief engi-
neer, e. M. Garland, and his stokers
and engineers tackled the blaze at
close quarters. Fourteen coal passers
and fourteen men In the engine room
were ordered to keep the ships boiler
fires going.


Crew Kept Back With Guns.

these men. Filipinos for the most part,
became panicstricken and wanted to
make a rush for the boats. Edward
Standish and Eugene Topping. assistant
kept them at work.

platforms over the sides. broke in the
ports of the burning compartment with
sledge hammers and fought with lines
of hose.


At one time it seemed that to save
the lives of the 1874 passengers and the
crew of more than two hundred it
would be necessary to beach the ship
on the Dutch coast. but Capt. Mcleod
determined to hang on. Meanwhile the
many streams OF water pouring into the
hold had become too much for the bilge
pumps and the ship was settling in the

to starboard. which kept the water
away from the flames.

Dublin gave evidence this week that

Details Of negotiations for one of the
e1rgest transatlantic cargo contracts
Of the year. in which the Shipping
Board lost to the Holland America
Line, the Reardon-Smith Line and the
United American Lines, became public
yesterday. The contract concerned the
movement of provisions from the
United States TO Rotterdam and Ham
burg, and involved shipments aggre-
eating many millions of dollars in
value.


When the Continental Conferences
was disrupted last spring and the
rates on provisions. among other COM
modities, we're thrown open, there WAS
q rush among the steamship lines to
close long contracts at the best possi~
Die rates. The biggest prize OF the lot
was the movement Of packing products.


When the scramble was over it was
found that the Reardon-Smith Line and
the United American Lines, which has
joint service with the Hamburg
American, had obtained practically all
the business to Hamburg. The Hol~
land-America Line had closed the con-
tract for Rotterdam. The Shipping
Board came out with empty hands.


AS reported yesterday, the board
then demanded that the Holland-Amer-
ica Line split the contract under PEN
atty of rate war. After some delib-
Grafton the company, which had been
dealing with the packers for many
Years, put the issue before them and
asked them If they wished to turn over
half the movement to the board. The
packers refused to give their consent,
saying that they were content with the
contract as it stood.


The Shipping Board temporarily put
into effect its threat of a rate war, re-
ducing the provision rate to Is cents
FOR 100 pounds, but later restored the
tariff to 20 cents, AS the matter
stands now, the foreign fines have the
greater part of the business.


At the time the negotiations were
under way several weeks ago, consid-
cradle secrecy was preserved by Ship
ping Board officials, who admitted that
important discussions were under way,
but refused to give out details.

Special Dispatch TO The Star.


NEW YORK, May 6.-The winter OF
the farmers discomfort has not been
made glorious summer yet. but 1t has
blossomed into promising spring.
Money. real hard coin, Is coming into
their hands and the future gives no
indication that their profits will be
checked. Cotton has had Its first real
move for months and that move HAS
been upward. Weather conditions
and crop prospects are inducing the
agriculturists of the south to talk
hopefully of 20-cent cotton and the
jump has given opportunity to many
to turn old holdings into cash.


Grain. strengthened by the prospect
OF Increased world demand and short
supply. Is maintaining it's strength.
and trains and vessels are pouring
their cargoeS into shipping and mill
ing centers and the returns into the
farmers pockets. Shipments of the
early vegetables and berries are IN
full swing in the south, and the sea-
son is gradually working northward.
with ready cash following in Its wake.


Permanence of Betterment.


The west may not be wild any long
er. but it Is woolly, and glad of 1t.



kalispell. Mont. are cashing the fat
checks for their clips. sold at prices
averaging nearly double what they
obtained last year. The live stock
situation is improving. and the ranges
and pastures are flush with feed and
water.


Business In general has just begun
to feel the effects of this distribution
of ready cash, but those effects Will
be increasingly evident from now on.
The first returns to the farmer have
gone to pay his debts. Old loans are
being rapidly cleared off and for the
first time since the depression, be-
came acute. the agriculturist feels he
has money to spend. The, mail order
houses have marked this first and
now the retail merchants are begin
ming to reap their harvest. They are
rejecting the feeling Of confidence in
the permanence of betterment.


Textile Trades Active.


The rise in basic materials has been
followed by renewed activity in the
finished products. especially in the
textile trades. Cotton goods have
in price are predicted. Consumers. 1t
appears, are willing to buy. but mills
are not anxious to sell for future
delivery until the price of raw cotton
has stabilized itself. Woolen goods
and worsteds have risen.


Manufacturers in many districts and
many industries are buying raw ma
terials and turning out finished prod
ucts for future, as well as present
demand. Orders for mill and factory
supplies are increasing steadily and
many makers of such goods are
booked months ahead. Lumber pro-
duction. although speeded up in every
producing section. cannot keep pace
with new business engendered by
building activity.


Gasoline has been advanced In price
and further advances are forecast.
The reverberatories of the copper
smelters are beginning to roar again.
and the ore and concentrates are
pouring in as production is being
resumed at the mines. Zinc and lead
also are in better technical positions.


Auto Trade Striking Example.


The revival Of the automobile in
dustry perhaps offers the most strik-
ing example of industrial improve
ment. Manufacturers are behind
with deliveries and are increasing
their forces and working hours In
desperate effort to take the tide of
business at the flood. Their chief
worry is to secure sufficient parts
ure production without carrying bur-
densome inventories. There is prom
ise that the automotive Industry
will experience the biggest year in
it's history.


Steel production is increasing
slightly despite the coal strike.
Plants are Well booked ahead, many
have withdrawn from the market,
and prices are trending upward from
pig iron to the finished product. To
say. however, that the coal strike has
not affected commerce and industry
is like telling the patient in dem
fists chair that he will not feel the
twist of the forceps.


The Suitcase" population, the
itinerate workers both skilled and
unskilled, are gradually settling
down to steady jobs for the summer
either in the industrial centers or on
the farms

Princess Newana Gayfish, Winuebago
Indian beauty of Hatfield. Wis. upset
a thousand years of tradition and her
own domestic life when she bobbed
her hair and introduced her fellow
red men to flapperism. Her father,
Chief Running Wolf. and her hus-
band, Dan Gayfish. put on war dance
that made the silent forests sound
like a reunion of boilermakers.


After the storm had cleared Newana
found herself an exile so far as her
relatives were concerned. But, not
being easily disturbed. she accepted
her misfortune with smile and that
evening she and her baby son turned
their backs on the old reservation
and went to Nebraska. where an un-
Gle left her $4,000 and a large trac.
of land. She will attempt to cultivate
the land.


Newana is eighteen years old and
has been married three years.

tificate. The Messaggero comments upon

PARIS, Jan. % ASSOCIATED Press).-
The passing of Pope Benedict Is treated
by Paris newspapers not only from the
religious and humanitarian but from a
political viewpoint The story OF the
vatican's efforts in the war is widely
retold, all the papers regrettiHg the Pope
did not show more openly the sympathy
with the Allies which most OF them con-
cede he possessed to a greater or less de-
gree.


Benedict XIV. left with those who had
seen and known him the memory of a
gentle soul and meditative intelligence"
says the Temps. neither OF which was
I'm place amid the crash OF the years or
iron and fire that his papacy covered"


The Temps wishes that full play might
have been given his peaceful ability and
his genuine kindliness in other than
war time, and suggests that Benedict
should have been Pope during the in
cumbency held by Plus Y. and that
Pius's flame should have lighted the
Vatican during the war.


The Journal des .Debuts in two and
q half column editorial analyses Pope
Benedict's diplomacy and career; it re-
iterates similar regrets, expressing the
opinion the Pope during the war was
badly informed. badly counseled and
badly obeyed."


But full praise is vouchsafed the
Pope's personal virtues and high intel
ligence, although. in the view OF the
paper "he rarely mastered questions
with that vast and rapid intuition that
characterizes great statesmen"


The Debdts concludes by asserting the
Pope lacked invcntiveness and force
fulness," and, facing the world up
heaval, "he was an attentive and
moved observer rather than resolute
and efficacious actor.


He had the intention Of doing some
great things, the accomplishment of
which obviously exceeded his powers"
adds the paper, land which others per-
haps will seek to achieve


All the papers look hopefully to the
selection OF his successor Some regret
that Frances influence has diminished
of late, as three of her Cardinals,
Annette. Debourg and Carriere, who died.
have not yet been replaced.


All the papers pay tribute to his con-
ciliatory attitude, resulting in the re-
sumption of diplomatic relations between
France and the Vatican last year. and
removing the difficulties dating back to
1905. when separation OF the church
and state In France took place.


The diplomatic dinner and reception
at the Elysee Palace, which had been
arranged for Wednesday. has been
countermanded. Premier Poncarc and
NJ. Defouqueres, master OF protocol,
called at the Nupcaturc this afternoon
to offer the Governments condolences.

Two days before Christmas the

How many among the crowds that attended

the dead. But such European customs never will
have place IN this country We are not ancestor

wrecked mile east of Gary, Ind. Of
ficials Of the road charge that the
spikes had been drawn from the rails

and Z. Lubbs, respectively engineer and
fireman Of the train, whose bodies were
buried in the wreckage Of the engine.

and A. B. Heath, express messengers.

cars, was speeding sixty miles an hour

jumped the rails, plowed along the ties

gage car, carried along by the momen-
tum of the other cars behind it, went
200 feet beyond the engine before it
toppled into the ditch, mass of wreck
age. All told, five cars were smashed
and ten ditched.

agents of the road swarmed to the
scene from Gary, and it was from these
agents that the officials obtained the
evidence which purported to show that
the wreck was the work Of strikers or
their sympathizers. According to Cap
tain Martin Quinn, chief special agent,
his men found that the spikes which
hold the rails to the ties had been
pulled from about thirty-seven ties.


Officials Of the road have offered a
reward of $1,000 for the arrest of the
persons responsible for the wreck.

That Near East peace conference had

porary depression and Partisan brok-

JACKSON. Cal. Sept. le.-The
bodies Of the forty-seven Argonaut
miners are coming out of the
ground. Arrangements are being
made for inquest and for funerals.
The story has been told.


There is but one thing left to tell
the love story Of Charley Fsz-
gerald, one of the forty-seven, and
Emily Brown.


Fitzgerald lived for many years
In Jackson with his wife. They
had two children. One day Mrs.
Fitzgerald left her husband and
hildren-and IL was a long time un-
Til Emily came to mother them.
Emily fell in love with Charley.
he braved everything. that she
might care for him and his chill
dren. The neighbors treated her
kindly and calld eer Mrse. Fitz-
gerald


Six months they lived thus. Then
the fire broke out In the Argonaut
mine and trapped Fitzgerald and his
forty-six comrades. The charity
workers came to Jackson. They
too. treated Emily as though she
were Mrs. Fitzgerald-until the real
Mrs. Fitzgerald came back TO
jackson.


Her coming made a difference in
Emily's position. The pay check
that was to have gone TO Emily
did not go to her. The money to
be awarded by the State Industrial
Accident Commission will not go
to Emily. Mrs. Fitzgerald made Il
clear that she wanted the money.
rot for herself. but for her children.
Incidentally. she took the check
away from Emily. Emily began TO
be treated as an outcast. Only Mrs.
Murphy. next door. saw anything
of her during the last few weeks
of the search for the bodies.


Mrs. Murphy and Emily weer out
at the mine lass night when the
news came in. Mrs. Murphy's hus-
band. coming up from the sepulchre,
broke the news gently. Emily went
home without a word. She had
hoped that Charley would come
back from the dead. But with
Charley gone from her and Char
ley's children and even his name
taken from her-she felt the end
had come. She swallowed a bottle
OF lysol.


Mrs. Murphy had suspected Emily
would try suicide and arrived just
In time 60 get a doctor and save
the girls life. She will recover
the doctor says.

TRENTON, Aug. 21.-Convicts Of the
New Jersey State Prison, after day
OF violence and disorder, are in spirit
OF revolt tonight which even the pres
ence of troop Of State Police, score
of local police and every available dep
ut;- keeper has not subdued.


n The rebellion among the convicts
started last night and grew out of dis
satisfaction with their supper. They
have since been in hostile spirit and
the climax was reached late this after
noon, when 600 Of them refused to obey
orders Of deputies TO march into their
cells from the exercising yard.


Violence followed, and SO serious did
the situation become that it was neces-
sary for Headkeeper Joseph s. Hoff to
send an emergency call to State Police
Headquarters and to the Trenton police
for assistance in controlling the out
break.


Peach Portion Called Scanty


The convicts started demonstra-
tion last night upon returning to their
cells from the mess hall. Peaches had
been served FOR dessert and their com
plant was that the quantity was in
sufficient. Each man was given sim
gle peach. but this: did not satisfy
them. The conventional convict meth
DDS of registering dissatisfaction by
knocking tin cups onS cell bars fol-
lowed, and this was augmented by
yells and screams which continued
during the night.


Throughout the morning and early
part OF the afternoon there was COM
parative peace, but the dieorder was
renewed on more violent scale when
1T came time to turn the seven hun
dree men who were out in the yard
exc. %ssing back into the cell tiers.
They sent up wall of defiance that
could be heard several blocks. Finally
about hundred yielded to the de-
mands and threats of the deputies and
started into the building.


The remaining 600 or more took up
stones and threw them at the men who
had. deserted their ranks, cutting and
bruising many of them. They de-
manded that the principal keeper come
out to them, but he refused to treat
Win eHe luutlHeeTS excepting through
a committee and only after they had
returned to their cells. This decision
resulted in another outbreak and "a
call was then sent in for outside help.


Rcvolvers Cow Men


With drawn revolvers more than 100
offers surrounded the mutineer con-
victs and drove them into their cells
There the disorder was continued and
the convicts during the night smashed
the electric light bulbs outside their
cells and broke practically everything
that could be destroyed. They
screamed and kept up continual din,
and finally the entire prison was
thrown into darkness in the hope of
quieting the men.


Officers of the prison have succeeded
in determining many Of the ringlead-
ers in the rioting, and have marked
them for severe punishment. They
are somewhat at loss to explain the
demonstrations Of violence, which
have been among the most serious in
the history of the institution. 1t is
attributed in some measure to the fact
that the institution Is overcrowded,
the population Of the prison now being
1921, and to the fact that the men
have been suffering greatly during the
last few days from the excas siye heat

Forty men last night took possession

Parnell street quietly conducted the
rishtful occupants TO the street and then
closed the doors of the building. The
men were still in possession this eve
ming. 1t was said they had been identi-

Belfast. The interlopers are reported to
have taken food into the building with
them. One report during the day was
that the building had been Communicated
by the Irish Republican Army.


The taking over OF Orange Hall was
the first instance of such an attack on
southern Orangemen as retaliation for
the treatment to which Nationalists have
been subject in Belfast. 1t Is a large
and handsome building, and had been
prepared Saturday night for a dance
and supper. When the seizure took place
the occupants OF the hall were expelled
and the Belfast Nationalist workmen.
who are now destitute in Dublin through
having been discharged from the ship
yards, ate the supper prepared for the
Orangemen. The Metropolitan Police did
not attempt to disturb the invaders.


Later Fowler Memorial Hall, the city
fish market and the war materials stored
there were seized. 1t is not known as
yet whether all the seizures were carried
out by the same forces. The taking over
OF Orange Hall seemed to be sympathet-
ically greeted by the populace to-day.

smartly to its close, the skies will
soon be shipping some novelties in
SHOWS; and all the bathing peaches
have left the ocean beaches. and
through the woodland reaches a
keen wind shrewdly blows. There's
something sad and drcary about the
days of fall; they're seldom bright
and CHEEKY, spring days they don't
recall; the nights are long and
chilly; the roads are rough and
hilly; along them Weary Willie
hunts for winter stall. We face
increased expenses, though we are
in the hole; we'll have to burn the
fences, so costly is the coal; the
price OF grub is sleeper: and yet.
why be weeper? For rubber tires
are cheaper, and still our busses
roll. We'd dodge a lot of sorrow
and woe that makes us yell, if we'd
vacate tomorrow the shacks in
which we dwell. old ties and Gus
toms sever. old forms of dull en-
deavor, and in our cars forever
abide till life's farewell. Why should
we live in shanties. and pay for heat
and light, and bonnets for our
aunties. and everything we bitter
The long white road is lying out
doors where wheels are flying, and
motor horns are ofying-why not
pull out tonight? Thus foolishly !
twitter; such vagrant dreams will
come, when autumn winds are bit
ter, and life seems out of plumb;
when | can't rightly figure. as bills
grow big and bigger, just how I'll
stand the rigor of winter, bleak and
glum.

Jeffrey Wilson of Rochester was res

bridge.

too short. Several ladders with ropes
attached were lowered. but lodged
among rocks before reaching Wilson

rope held by Patrol Driver Charles Rad
ford on the bank. About 100 feet from

his footing and worked his way to a
rock few feet from Wilson. Smith
urged Wilson to jump to his arms and
the policeman caught him. The trip
back to shore was a slow struggle
against the swift current.

and denied he had attempted suicide.

text:
The East Side paid tribute en- masse
yesterday to the memory of Bernard
Bernstein, the Jewish actor.


Twenty thousand mourners crowded
the Bowery as the funeral cortege
slowly moved along, hating for a few
minutes at each of the theatres at
which Bernstein had played his mimi
table comedy roles. A hundred police
keep them from breaking up the
organized procession behind the hearse.
A compact mass followed the body of
their histrionic idol through the
streets. The Bowery seemed to be
animated as the dense throng swept
everything before it.


The crowd was quiet one. They
formed outside the Hebrew Actors
Club, 108 Second Avenue, where the
body had been lying in state since
Friday. Services were held there and
Cantor Samuel Misles chanted a hymn
to the dead comedian. All the while
masses of mourners came pouring into
the neighborhood and Captain Peter
utilized fifty unmounted and ten
mounted patrolmen to keep them from
surging into the already overcrowded
club.


After the services the procession got
under way. The pallbearers were six
actor friends of Bernstein. The coffin
was taken to the Kessler Theater, six
blocks away, where it was put on the
stage 10 enable severa. thousand per-
cons to pass by the bier. The crush be-
came so great that the police finally
had to close the doors of the theater
where Bernstein for years played to
capacity audiences.


The coffin was then placed in hearse
and the cortege began to move toward
Houston Street, with brief halt at
every Jewish theater along the Bowery.
At the Warsaw Synagogue on Rivington
Street short ceremony was conducted
and then the procession headed for the
Williamsburg Bridge. The crowd
the bridge and when Mount Zion Gene
terry was reached there were compare
lively few who witnessed the inter
ment. Bernstein was buried in the
section of the. cemetery occupied by
the Warsaw Sick and Benevolent So
ciety.


The beloved Jewish actor was born
in Lcmberg, Galicia, sixty-one years
ago. He came to this country thirty
one years ago and his career perhaps
has no parallel on the jewish speaking
stage. He died last Tuesday at the
Lenox Hospital following a brief i'll
ness.


Bernstein Is survived by his wife,
three daughters and two sons, known
professionally as Herman and Fred
Berrens.

These Ozark people, by all modern
standards, are without musical train
ing. They are largely descendants

tic coast who moved westward along

and Tennessee. They are cohserva-
tives who have preserved carefully
early American traditions. They sing
as their forefathers sang in New
England, Virginia, Kentucky and at
those great revivals OF militant
Christianity and hymn singing OF
which PETER CARTWRIGHT and other
pioneer evangelists were the leaders.
In their singing they perhaps come
nearer than any other persons to per-

park, the Cleveland field and the Chi

which would be most affected.

ceed that figure. but in the opinion of

To THE NEW YORK HERALD: John
Philip Sousa's reference to the old mys-
terry of who struck Billy Patterson re-
calls the only explanation I ever heard
of the cause for that much repeated
query.


In June OF 1894, while camping in the
Yosemite Valley with Herbert Hoover
and other college associates. we got UP
a great campfire gathering, to which
were summoned only the college folk then
among the hundreds of campers in that
wonderful valley. Our campfire was in
natural amphitheater under the Royal
Arches, up near Mirror Lake and close
beside the icy Merced River. The reg
lstry that night showed men and women
present from thirty-seven different col
leges of America and Europe.


James Brett Stokes, Princeton 81, n
related the story responsible for the
question who struck Billy Patterson"


In years gone by there was an annual
feud night conflict between the univer-
sity students at oxford and the river
boatmen. Billy Patterson was the rec
ognized leader among the boa tmen and
a bruiser to be dreaded. To capture
him became the special object Of the
English collegians.


This was effected. Billy was hurried
away one rush night to an awesome
chamber There all the assembled were
in black gowns and cowls and were
masked. A mock tribunal was insti-
tuted. Billy was tried, found guilty,
sentenced He was to be guillotined
The beheading block was revealed, the
headsman stood beside 1t with huge
battle-ax.


Billy bound hand and foot, was placed
kneeling before the curved depression
and his throat fitted down into 1t and
the blindfold placed over his eyes The
command was given. The blow fell upon
Bnly's powerful neck. 1t was only a
cord that had been wet in cold water.
Billy remained inert. Moments passed.
Billy had tainted? No, Billy was dead.


The whole thing had been very real to
HIM. His heart had stopped for all
time. The affrighted students removed
their disguses. spirited the body out to
the rivers edge and left It.


who struck Billy Patterson" re.
mains mystery. ARCHIE RICE


NEW York, August 23.

books. Notwithstanding the improve

Two decisions Of the Police Court un-
der the "vagrancy" law were reversed
today by the District Court of Appeals

Justice Robb.


The chief justice held that Hilda Rose
was wrongfully convicted when the tes-
timony showed that she had $1,000 to
her credit in bank. 1t was the duty
of the prosecution to show that the
amount was not sufficient for her sup
port and not merely to question the
method by which the money was ac-
cumulated. the court held: That the
woman might have been charged with
some other crime does not make her .
vagrant. The costs Of the appeal were
assessed against the District.


In the other case, in which Justice
Robb read the courts opinion. the con-
viction of Lucretia Lewis was set aside.
The testimony here showed that the
woman was regularly employed as
housekeeper at weekly stipend Of $40.
board and lodging. The fact that her
employers house had been suspected
by the police does not make her amen
able to the vagrancy act, the court
stated.

STOCKHOLM. February 2.-Three
weeks of incessant freezing weather
have formed ice in the Baltic sea so
thick as to interfere seriously with
navigation.


Pack ice. often more than fifteen
feet thick. has been forced into Swe-
den's eastern harbors. blocking all
ports north of Stockholm. All the
Finnish ports also are blockaded.


Ice covers the sea for hundreds OF
miles, and many steamships are pro-
ceeding to the Swedish archipelago to
escape it's menace. The American
steamship Eastern Coast. bound for
Reval. is among the vessels seeking
refuge in Swedish waters from the
ice drift.


Finnish and Swedish ice breakers
are working to their utmost to keep
the harbors Of this port and Reval
open. The latter Is seriously threat
ened.

advancing from the southwest at 5:45.

ing his attentive ears was recorded at

The Cafe Royal, which has catered
TO those who know fine cooking and
loved good wines for more than sixty
years and has been the resort of promi-
nent men in the life of England and the
Continent, will soon pass into history.
The old establishment. where one can
still find the fastest game of dominoes
and the finest wine in London. was con-
demned pending reconstruction with
other premises under the plan for re-
building Regent street.


Daniel Nicholas de Nicol made the
Cafe Royal famous with his excellent
cuisine and remarkable cellar, but most
o. all by fostering the atmosphere or
art which characterizes the place to-day.
For half a century 1t has been known as
the headquarters for the more prominent
Frenchmen in London and the followers
of Napoleon III. who planned his exile
met here De Nicol came to London as
a poor waiter and died q millionaire
after the war.


Among the celebrities who made the
place their club in their humble days
were Henri Rochefort. Aubrey Boards
ley, Augustus Johns. Epstein and Paul
verlaine. 1t is also said to have heen a
favorite haunt of South American reb-
els, Irish conspirators. poets, prize
fighters and financiers


The gay side of London's night life
found expression here with Continen-
tai background with youth OF both sexes
drinking champagne while the bon-viv-
ant slipped his Chateau Lafitte or his
Pommard


The reconstruction will include a
gilded ballroom. a hotel and other i'm
provements' which the habitues declare
viii mean the end of the Cafe Royal.

The hootleggers who sneaked on
board the Homeric just after she
docked yesterday, loaded their pockets
with bottles of whisky, ran across a
pier filled with officers, jumped into
their motor-boat and made away under
fusillade of bullets from customs
guard, all in broad daylight, are, in
the estimation of prohibition enforce
ment officials, just about the boldest in
their profession so far.


Their presence was first noticed by
the crowd on the pier when, in the
midst Of the examination of the bag
gage of passengers from the Homeric,
there was series of shots from the
end of the pier. Those who ran to the
south side to ascertain the cause saw
fifty-foot gray motor launch, with
seven occupants, scurrying at full
speed out into the river from between
Piers 5S and So. Customs Guard
Charles Ostman. it developed, had seen
several men hurrying across the lower
deck of the pier from the Homeric
with their coats bulging. When he
called to them to halt they hurried
only the faster and jumped into the
boat tied alongside the pier with its
engine running and a man at the
throttle.


When the rum runners got fifty feet
away they stopped and called out that
they wanted to have talk with Ost-
man. The latter's reply was three
shots from his pistol, fired over their
heads.


"Well get you for that" they cried
and, ducking below the gunwales,
made off into the river. Ostman an
swered that the next time he would
shoot to kill, and fired several bullets
into the launchs hull, without apparent
effect, however. With Ostman was
James Nolan, another guard, who took
off his coat and was about to swim
after the craft when he became con-
vinced that such a pursuit would be
useless, as the boat was rapidly being
lost to sight in the river traffic.


Customs authorities said that the
rum runners We're evidently in conspir-
acy with some of the Homeric's crew,
and that they probably got aboard the
ship from the off side, as she was be-
ing warped into her pier. The motor
boat which escaped, it was said, was
one of a fleet of six which was stand
ing off the end of Pier SO waiting for a
chance to get in. Much liquor has dis
appeared from passenger ships after
dark, say the customs men, but never
before has daylight attempt been
made. They estimated that each of
the men who got away yesterday was
probably carrying with him at least
twelve bottles OF whisky.

Special Dispatch to THE New York HERALD


CAPE MAY. N. j.. May 1.-THE men
who have been fighting the forest fires
that are raging in Atlantic. Cape May
and Cumberland counties have gone
on strike for higher wages, and with
their aid gone the fire wardens are
not able to make Roadway against the
flames. Tonight the fires are burning
fiercely in the vicinity Of Woodbine.
with every likelihood that they will
spread into sections of the timber
lands hitherto untouched. WIS.,


1t was while fighting the flames at
Woodbne that the fire fighters threw
down their brooms and shovels and
walked out Of the forest. declaring that
they would not return until their wages
had been raised. They are now being
paid at the rate of $50 for three hours
work, and 80 cents an hour for every
hour they work after three hours. They
struck for rs cents an hour. and quit
when they were told 1t would not be
paid. They declare they can make more
than 35 cents an hour working in the
Woodbine mills and on the farms of
south Jersey.


Fire fighting is done in gangs of eight
men or boys, six with broons, which
they use in beating out the flames in the
underbrush, and two with shovels, with
which they dig bitches around houses
and across open spaces to keep the fire
from spreading. This method has not
been very successful during the last week
in south Jersey. The fire has been burn
ing near Woodbine for nearly a week,
and the fire fighters have been working
almost continually.


The flames burned so fiercely last
night that they illuminated the country
for miles around as brightly as daylight.
The town of Steelmanton has been saved
by bitches and by using all methods Of
fighting forest fires, but fears are enter
tanned for the safety of other small set
Elements In the woods near Tuckahoe


The fire has already burned from just
outside of Woodbine to Marshallville
road, a distance of four miles Another
fire Is burning near Newtonville on the
Cape May division Of the Reading, and
unless the wind dies down several houses
will be burned The smoke was so thick
last night between Woodbine and Tucka-
hoe that automobilists could not use the
roads.


The fires have ruined the huckleber-
ries. and Game Warden William Steele
said to-day that there probably would be
no berries at all in south Jersey this
year This will be especially hard on
many families that live In the woods and
at certain seasons of the year depend
on berries for their livelihood.


Warden Steele said also that the fires
have practically exterminated small
game In some sections of Cape May
county. Dead rabbits are scattered
along the roads, and the deer have run
into the towns and the farm yards for
safety.


IT is estimated that the damage in
Cape May Atlantic and Cumberland
counties will aggregate more than ST.
000, 900.

Happy Ireland and thrice happy

long dream come true For England

"Tommies" swung down the Dublin

ireland must now seek another vic
