CoNSTANTINOPLE, Sept. 2S
(By The Associated Press) Events
are surely approaching climax.
The Turks have occupied the entire
neutral zone on the Asiatic side of
the Dardanelles, with the exception
of the Chanak area, around which
they have established infantry units
in seni-circle, virtually investing
the British lines.


. The Turkish cavalry squadrons
are retiring, and the British troops,
who are in strong force at Chanak,
are ready for what may happen.


In these circumstances General
Harrington, the British commander
in chief, has sent wireless message
to Kenal Pasha at Smyrna, asking
for an immediate personal meeting
He leaves the choice of place to
Kemal, whose reply is expected mo-
mentarily.


Turks Push Martial Program


Yussuf Kemal Pasha, the Nationalist
Foreign Minister, is understood to have
gone to Angora to submit the Allied
joint note to the Nationalist Assembly,
but in the mean time Turkish concen-
trations are being pushed with the
greatest speed


British relnforcements are reaching
here and the threatened area The
super Revenge and Rev
olution, the most powerful fighting ma
chimes afioat, have arrived in the Dar-
danelles, while a battalion of North
staffordshires and 1000 men of the
British air forces landed to-day and
marched through Constantinople with
helped to bring about reassuring
effect.


Two thousand British marines and
Grenadier Guards and two battalions
Of Dorsets are due here to-morre%.


The Turkish instructions to the men
in the Chanak sector are to advance
the farthest possible without meeting
resistance. They are now practically
against the British intrenchments, and
obviously the situation cannot be in
definitely prolonged.


notwithstanding the Kemalist con-
centrations around Chanak. however,
the British are confident of holding
their lines against all odds. They de-
clare that their flanks are we'll pro-
tected by the fleet. The battleships,
with their 16-inch guns, can sweep the
whole area around Chanak for a dis
tance of twenty miles, and it is pos
sible for the British to dismount some
of their giant naval guns and use them
for shore batteries.


The Turks at present have only
machine guns in the Chanak area If
they brought up heavy artillery the
security of Chanak might be seriously
challenged, the British admit, but the
entrenchments in this sector are said
to be more efficient than any used in
the World War. Since September II
1000 men from the labor squad, 1000
from the fleet and several thousand
from the army have been steadily
building trenches and setting up gun
emplacements.

Joe Lynch. the West Side bantam and
former holder Of the worlds title. earned
championship match with Johnny Buff
last night In Madison Square Garden by
giving trouncing to Midget Smith, who
also harbored ambitious plans. The bout
went twelve rounds.


Lynch defeated Smith with left hand
attack that would have aroused the ad-
miration of Jim Corbett. and Johnny
Buff. the present title holder. who
watched the contest from the ringside
seat. was duly impressed with the man
ner of Lynch's victory. Lynch shot his
trusty left into Smiths face with such
precision and regularity that the little
chap was soon bleeding profusely from
mouth and nose.


Smith tried desperately from start to
finish to get a solid right handler on
Lynchs jaw but most of his efforts
merely grazed the mark, and had no
damaging effect on the West Slider.


The bout as a whole was extremely
interesting, being full of action. and both
men evidently trying. their best. Smith
forced the pace in the early rounds and
led in points for considerable time.
He hooked his right to Lynch's face at
frequent intervals and also used the
same hand on Lynch's body when
at close quarters Lynch apparently
played waiting game until the seventh
round when he cut loose and with a
stinging left handler to the face and
heavy right hooks to the jaw staggered
the midget and had him in distress at
the bell.

hour preceding dark?

above the graceful limbs of the will
low trees, apparently never descend
ing to the ground after the sun has
set. A light breeze blows the entire
column few feet from the trees
over which they hover, but they fly
pack, never disturbing the symmetry
of the tall insect spire Perhaps they
settle down on the leaves after dark.
and perhaps tho moving spire seen
on warm nights over the trees on the
speedway is merely the evening con-
stititional of the insect host.


At any rate they have attracted the
attention and interest of hundreds
of motorists, who would probably be
glad to have the bureau of entomo- =
logy explain their weird gyrations
over the willow trees.

INDIANAPOLIS, Nov. 4.-With their
engine belching smoke and about to
burst into flames. Lieuts. John Ma
cready and Oakley Kelly were forced
to end their ocean to ocean nonstop
monoplane flight at Fort Benjamin
Harrison at 9:15 A. M. to-day.


The aviators had used all their cof-
fee, soup and condensed milk in a vain
effort to cool their overheated engine
the water for the purpose having
leaked through cracked water Jacket.


Lieut.. ]. e. Parker. in command of

The men in the big monoplane left
San Diego at $3.50 A. NJ. Friday.
Swinging out through Arizona and
New Mexico to avoid the mountains
and deserts. they covered 1850 miles
OF the 1850 miles to New York. Diff
ficult head winds and cold weather
bothered them.


While the men did not reach their
goal, the Atlantic Coast, they established
a record for nonstop flying.


Trouble Two Hours Out.


Engine troubles developed less than
two hours out Of San Diego Friday, but
rather than give up the flight, the two
officers agreed to stick with the ship"
when the water jacket of cylinder on
the right side of the engine cracked.
That was the first trouble. Twelve hours
of running with the engine wide open
caused the jackets of other cylinders to
crack. the water being lost gradually
from the radiator.


With the trouble in the engine con-
tinually developing. the officers drove
their plane over hundreds of miles of
mountains, wherep safe landing was
impossible and then over many more
miles of desert where a landing also
would have meant death.


When the trouble was discovered, they
might easily have turned back to San
Diego. Instead their agreement held
them to their task and they continued
toward their goal


The course mapped out for their fight
would have taken them across central
Indiana, about ten miles south of Indian
apols. but the engine was performing
so badly when they came into Indiana
that they headed for the flying field at
Fort Harrison and landed. The engine
would not have carried them much
further.

Some competent observers believe

In general German industry is re-
ducing production. The principal reason
for this Is the difficulty of getting bank
credits. Three months ago German
banks began cutting down the credits
they advanced to old enterprises and
to refuse money to new ones. To-day
the banks are Withdrawing part of the

Until the prices of German COM

German factories cannot manufacture

and other manufacturers admit that
rise in the mark would paralyze in
dustry.


The textile industry offers a typical
example of present conditions. The
price Of cotton in Bremen rose parallel
with the mark. The price now is about
30 per cent. higher than on June /. But
the manufacturers, despite the increase,
bought heavily, expecting the mark to
collapse. The retailers also flooded the
wholesalers with orders. The cotton in
dustry is booked solid until the end OF
October with the deliveries extending
into March. Only momentary failure
to get sufficient cotton prevented the
manufacturers from taking on more
orders. But this industry would become
a highly speculative and disastrous one
were the mark to take any other course
than slow depreciation in value.


Textile manufacturers. especially
manufacturers Of wooden goods, tell THE
NEw YORK HERALD correspondent that
they have begun steady reduction in
their output this year. Several old
firms have failed and others-dc not feel
that they can carry on under the heavy
speculative chances due to the mark
fluctuations. The retailers have, now
organized cartel and will negotiate
with the manufacturers as unit. Deals
are closed when the raw materials are

A threatened coal strike in the Ruhr
district was avoided through compro-
misses In which the employers agreed not
to ask for overtime work and granted

many will have only $4,000. 900 tons Of

TO the loss OF Upper Silesia and reduc-

The Allies have secured the financial
and export control over Germany which
they desired. The agreements made with
Berlin last week. The German Govern
ment must now supply the Allies with
statistics showing the country's resources
when desired. Without controlling Ger
nanys exports and imports, the Allies
can examine the detailed reports and
can recommend notifications. The most
important provision is the one which
gives the Allies the right to compel the
Germans to open their private books to
them II they suspect false export decla-
rations. The Allies are not limited in
their control. because they have direct
control over German commerce. industry
and customs. while the Government
merely exerts official supervision.


The principal objection of the Ger
mans to the extended control of the Al
lies is that Germany's business secrets

greatest rivals.

FORT WORTH. Tex, February 20.
Revival of business activity has
followed the rains throughout north,
south and east Texas, but trade in
west Texas still continues slow today
because of the drought in that sec
ton. The conditions in the extreme
northwestern countries are some
what better than on the plains, but
still are far from normal for this
period of the year. Grass on the
cattle ranges is playing out rapidly
and the stock raisers are being driven
to the expensive expedient of buying
feed.


Smelters around Ell Paso are COM
mencing to show signs of life as the
mines in Arizona and New Mexico are
resuming operations. The advance in
grain prices has materially cheered
the grain growers of the Texas pan
handle. VINO still hold large stocks.
Flour has made big net gains in all
the big milling centers within the
last week.


The Santa Fe and Frisco lines are
preparing to make large expendi-
lures for improvements throughout
the southwest and this will benefit
many laborers now unemployed. Or
ders have been issued at many points
on the Rock Island road to re-employ
forces laid off during January. The
Texas oil production for last week
showed a restriction of production of
5000 barrels a day from the figures
of the previous week.

BENJAMIN FRANKLIN'S birth
day, January II, is to receive more
than usual attention this year.


Franklin was the many-sided
American. And so, various kinds OF
trades and industries, professions and
organizations claim him as their
patron saint.


The printers and publishers make
the first claim. Poor Richards
Almanac was written by Richard
Saunders (pseudonym), but printed and
sold by B. Franklin, who cast the first
type, planned the first magazine and
printed the first novel in the colonies;
also establishing the Pennsylvania
Gazette, Of which the Philadelphia
North American is direct descendant


The booksellers claim him. Franklin
made books, but books made Franklin,
they say. And did Franklin not pub
lish the first booksellers catalog and
found the first circulating library?


Educational and literary interests
claim hin1-did he not found the Uni
versity Of Pennsylvania and Franklin
College, the latter now absorbed in
Franklin and Marshall College at
Lancaster, Pa; and is Franklin's
autobiography not a classic of
classics?


Science claims him as the mo,, aOho
snatched lightning from the skies.


Philosophy claims him. Even
music claims him as the inventor of
the armonica, an instrument that gave
music from glass discs. And state
craft acclaims him for his profound
and patriotic craftsmanship at home
and his marvellous diplomacy abroad.


But above all, the people-those
who read and think-find in Poor
Richards sayings the fountain of
common sense, sage counsel, homely
wisdom, and philosophy that helps
them over many rough paths in life.


Yes, Franklin was the many
sided American, and perhaps in
honoring his birthday we may find a
way to present some of the many
sides of the Wanamaker Store. Who
knows?


Keep thy shop, and thy shop a0iU keep
thee, is Franklin's first injunction to
the storekeeper. Drive My business;
let not that driue thee, is his second


The first saying is proved by our
more than 60 years of continuous
storekeeping. The second explains,
perhaps, our sometimes energetic
merchandising and advertising
methods

DUBLIN, July % (Associated Press) -
Glenveagh Castle. which for some time
has been the headquarters of rebels in
County Donegal and from which they
have conducted constant raids by rowing
bands. was captured by Free State
troops yesterday. Four separate con-
tingents converged at the castle early
In the morning and entered unopposed.
The eight occupants of the garrison were
taken prisoner, including d. j. Donovan,
chief OF the revel intelligence depart
ment and conductor OF the republican
"war bulletin" service.


The capture included, besides arms and
ammunition, important dispatches con-
tanning Information on the strength and
movements of rebels In that county. be-
sides a large quantity of merchandise
that had been looted from trains. The
Free State troops also captured twenty
four rebels nearby, who were believed
to have escaped from the castle while
the troops were approaching.


Free Staters captured the village or
Bruree. two miles from Kilmallock, last
night, together with the rebel occupants
of the village and their arms and am
munition. The rebels had established
a strong position there after their re-
treat from Limerick.


Two colonels and five soldiers OF the
Government forces were killed and
seven others wounded near Maryboro
last night by rebels. The colonels met
death during an ambush by the rebels.
while the other Free State troops were
killed when an armored car in which
they were proceeding to remove a mine
was blown up.


Reinforcements which arrived from
Maryboro were attacked by the rebels.
Three officers were wounded, two of
them fatally. Eighteen rebels were cap
;ured with arms and ammunition.


-Four hundred Free State troops who
left Thurles early yesterday were at
tackled near Golden Village by rebels.

WILMINGTON, N. c., Oct. 1.-THE big
circus elephant that escaped second
time here last night had disappeared to-
day in the sem-tropical jungle along
the Brunswick River.


The elephant swan the Cape Fear
River and at latest reports to the Will
mington police had penetrated far into
the swamps lying between Nhe Cape
Fear and the Brunswick. Three keep
ers went In pursuit, but the vegetation
is so dense and the danger from alliga-

stantly increasing obstacles.

but the property damage is estimated

parked automobiles.

George Menaker. forty.two years
old, was electrocuted when a short
circuit took place in the violet.ray
machine with which he was admins
tering a treatment to himself late
Yesterday afternoon. Across the
street, his fiancee, Miss Bertha Bod

Menaker, who for some time had

nick planned to celebrate Christmas
with Miss Bodnick's sister, Mrs. f.

niece, Marling.


After hiding the presents for Miss

fiancee a great surprise for Christ
mas. he hurried home to dress for

He then attached the violet-ray

hurriedly called District Detective

the house.

coiled around his body emitting
flashes.


Burns turned off the current and
after extricating the man sum
moned a nearby physician, who pro
nounced him head.


Miss Bodnick and Mrs. Sownetz
becoming impatient at Menaker'i
delay, were about to leave without
him and were sending a note to that
effect by Marlin when Mrs. Pettler
ran across the street and told them
to hurry to her house, as Menakei
was dead.


Miss Bodnick tainted and required
the attentions Of a physician, her
Christmas ruined and her marriage
frustrated.

The terse letter subjoined was re-
ceived yesterday.


ITO THE NEW York HERALD: Have
you gone crazy-to use full


column of the front page OF THE
HERALD to tell of boy who lost hisS
pup when the papers are all crowded
with important things?


"A FRIENDLY READER.


"NEw YORK. September 49,"


No, THE New YORK HERALD has not
gone crazy. Papers become demented
only when they lose track of the
human race and never put the boys
and the pups on the front page.


Our correspondent forgets the va
riety of news appetites. There are
ten thousand young men in New York
who could tell him how many home
runs Babe RUTH has made this year
but could not tell him whether Sou
tari is in Europe or in Asia. There
are a hundred thousand mothers in
New York who have not the slightest
interest in Southampton or Lenox but
who like to read about the boy and
the pup. For the boy might be their
own boy.


The world likes to read about
boys, and especially abo1t boys that
own pups The boy and the dog
have been pals since the axis of the
earth first began to creak under the
weight of the human race. There
were boys and pups before Babylon,
but Babylon and its brass gates have
gone and the boys and their pups re-
main. There will be lost boys with
lost pups, and kind policemen to find
and feed them, long after wars and
strikes have disappeared.


And so often as something happens
to boy and pup that makes the
world recall it's youth THE New YoR;I
HERALD will find room on the front
page for it, even if it has to relegate
the doings of some stodgy statesman
TO the inside

CHICAGO, Dec. 21.-Fire starting at a
few minutes before four o'clock this
afternoon destroyed the Dearborn street
railroad station. formerly known as the
Polk Street Depot, and left eight rail-
roads homeless In Chicago. The build
ing, erected in 1884. was valued at $780,
900. but will probably cost more than
s1.000,000 to replace.


Within a little more than an hour
after a traffic policeman saw smoke
issuing from the roof, the flames swept
through the structure, once the pride OF
railroad men. and left only a smoke
blackened brick shell behind.


Hundreds of passengers and 200 men
and women clerks fled to safety, but
Mrs. Hazel Locker. 26, woman clerk,
tainted and was trampled on by the wild
rush from the upper floors. A police
man found her lying unconscious on the
stairs and carried her out.


Postal clerks with motor trucks res
cued $50 tons of holiday mall. and rail-
road employees saved all passenger cars
in the trainsheds.


The station was owned by the Chi
cago and Western Indiana Railroad. and
was used by trains Of that line and the
Santa Fe, Monon, Erie, Chesapeake and
Ohio, Chicago and Eastern Illinois.
Wabash and Canadian Grand Trunk.


Crossed wires are believed to have
started the fire.

armistice has this city seen such
crowds and such enthusiasm.


There was monster procession.
The Paris post Of the American
Legion, which had failed to turn
out on the Fourth of July, marched
with the poilus.


At Longchamps. where there was
an imposing military review, the
crowds began to gather at vantage
points early in the day.


The picked troops of the French
republic began filing before the
tribunes at o'clock. There were
marines with broad, blue sailor col
lars, looking for all the world like
good children dressed for Sunday
school; two battalions of chasseurs,
just back from Upper Sllesia, where
they had been on police duty keep
ing the Poles and Germans from
each others throats; sharpshooters
from Indo. China; black troops from
the Senegal, very picturesque with
their bright uniforms and Jet black
face and their little red caps: but
the most interest was reserved for
the regulars-the ordinary French

forces and advanced from the North,
South and East. Artillery was en-

evacuate7 the city and withdraw rapidly
guard to engage the Nationals and de-

the National forces, however, this rear
guard hastened to join the retiring
main body.


Prior to leaving Clonmel the rebels

In this time Of sorrow Washington
remembers with gratefulness the
heroic services given in the hour of
stress by the employees Of the Chesa-
peake and Potomac Telephone Com
pany. In binding snowstorm, when
many other public utilities were forced
to suspend activities the telephones
were operated.


Then came the terrible catastrophe.
Like true heroines, in keeping with
the best traditions Of the company, the
telephone girls" kept the lines open,
answered the frenzied calls Of the
people, notified hospitals and doctors,
and in every way possible helped in
the work Of rescue.


Without the invaluable aid given by
the telephone service Saturday night
and Sunday morning it is difficult to
conceive what might have been the
state of affairs in connection with the
work of rescue at the knickerbocker
Theater. Doubtless many more lives
would have been lost. The city will
not soon forget what the telephone
service did, through storm and trag-
edy, and with the abnormal strain
upon the operators continuing, will
acknowledge its appreciation by exer-
cising patience and good nature over
the phone.

at the wheel of the dusty car. Mer-

ers. the Royal Scotch Fusiliers and the

toward the Irish Sea and home.

the evacuation OF Ireland by forces OF
the Crown will not begin until next
week. when Dublins own garrison will
march away with bands playing and
colors flying.

TO be withdrawn will leave here to-mor-
row night.

A dance in the Esperanza Club, at
500. persons had gathered, came to a
stop early yesterday when a party of
men who had entered and sought to
obtain dances started fights with the
girls partners and then began firing
revolvers. Fifteen shots were fred,
most Of which sank into the walls.
popped the electric lights or struck the
ceiling.


The firing stopped suddenly when a
girl 4nd man fell to the floor. both
wounded. They were Miss May Reilly,
10, a telephone operator. of $50 Eleventh
avenue, shot in the right shoulder and
Thomas O'Brien, 26, of 1900 Second ave-
nue.. struck in the right heel.


Two of the intruders had left one of
the refreshment tables near the dacing
floor and had seized two girls with a
request for a dance. Their partners
pushed the men aside and blows fol-
lowed. Then the trouble makers drew
revolvers and began firing.


At the first shot the orchestra halted
a fox trot and sought refuge. Some of
the dancers closed in and tried to knock
the weapons aside. In the struggle the
weapons were fired rapidly. lights
crashed and plaster broke from the
walls as the shots struck.


Then Miss Reilly dropped with cry.
and O'Brien went down. Women dancers
tainted. while the men ran to the in
jured. In the momentary lul! the two
armed men with their friends withdrew
toward the doors, holding the weapons
pointed at the nearest dancers. No one
tried to follow until the unwelcome Wis
ftors dashed through the doors. and
then dancers seized glassware from the
tables and hurled it and pursued the
intruders TO the street But the party
escaped.


Those left in the hall. recovering from
their fright. seized their wraps and
started for home. Some employees of
the hall called for help for Miss Reilly
and O'Brien. who were taken later to
Bellevue Hospital. Someone notified
the West Thirtieth street station. BY
the time the police arrived the place
was deserted except for the two In
Jured and some employees.


The police found two empty revolvers
in the hallway and about the dance hall
picked UP fifteen empty shells.

ARGONAUT MINE, JACKSON,

the Argonaut mine shaft. tomb of
forty-seven miners. alive or dead.
will finally be penetrated by the
rescue crews which have drilled.
blasted and dug increasingly for the
three weeks.


Belief that the penetration had
been accomplished in blast set off
at o'clock was dispelled when an
investigation showed that the blast
had ripped away nine feet Of rock.
opening up an unexpected porous
formation through which water was
seeping.


Although the Argonaut has not
yet been penetrated. the last blast

formations and miners are pushing

men entombed.


Need One More Blast.

stepped in this morning in the form
of a snowstorm and extinguished the
blaze.


Between 400 and 500 volunteer fire
fighters had found themselves unable
to cope with the fires because of the
high winds. and they had burned over
between 1000 and $500 acres when
the snowstorm broke over the county
early today. An inch of snow fell dur
ing the storm and extinguished the
fires, which have defied the fighters
for two days.

Marion, nl.-Indictments charging
thirty-eight men with murder were re
turned by the special grand jury In
vestigating the Herrin mine massacre.
Otis Clark was the first man to be in
dlcted and arrested. Leva Mann and
Charles Rogers, miners of Herrin; ;
Phillip Fontanetta, miner of Marion,
and James Brown, colored deputy, of
Colp, were also arrested. They are all
charged with murder. Officers had no
trouble making the arrests.


Col. Sam Hunter of the adjutant
generals office here, representing
Governor Small, said that quiet con
tinues over the county. He arrested
Phillip Fontanetta within ten minutes
after the names were given to the
sheriff and deputies. Many other ar
rests are expected.


Attorney General Brundage, in com
menting upon the action of the grand
jury, said that this special grand
jury of Williamson county has shown
through this partial report what the
luw-abiding people of this county think
of this massacre and of law enforce
ment."


The indictments cover a large terri
tory in y, illiamson and Franklin coun-
ties, and included in the list are at
least two officials-Constable John
Kelly of Zeigler, in Franklin county,
and Constable James Brown, who also
is deputy sheriff and chief of police
in the coIored mining camp of Colp.


The first Indictment accuses six men
of the Staying of Howard Hoffman of
Huntington, Ind, in the Herrin Gene
terry. He was one of the six captives
who escaped the massacre at the
barbed-wire fence in the timber. The
six were recaptured and led back to
the cemetery. They We're shot down.
One of them lived and the other five
died The men named in this true bill
are Peter Hitler, Clarence Rogers,
Leva Mann, Joseph Carneghi, Bert
Grace and Percy Hall.


The second Indictment names nine
men in connection with the hanging of
Robert j. Anderson, Sparta, Mich, at
the Southern Illinois strip mine. His
body was riddled with bullets after he
had been hanged. In the Indictment
there are two counts, one charging the
shooting and the other the hanging.
The men accused are Nava Cannady,
Herbert Rushing, Clyde Lee, james
Galligan, Bert Grace, Dallas McCree,
Otis Maynard, Joseph Rhodes and
William Stanley.


The third Indictment concerns the
Staying of John Shoemaker, son of
Mayor Shoemaker of Charleston, Ill.
He and thirteen other of the non-union
mine employees who had surrendered
under flag of truce, were killed at
the barbed-wide fence in the timber
near the power house. In this indict-
ment twenty-seven are made co-defend-
ants.

Indications are that the last has been

conflict recently between the middle

the national indoor title event in the
local armory and against the action Of
Vincent Richards in dcfaulting his
match In the latter tournament. The
regimental officials appear to have
judged the situation rather hastily and
to have protested before making sure Of
their facts. The controversy has proved
to be a tempest In teapot.


Had the Seventh Regiment Tennis
Club committee Investigated they would
have learned that the middle States
event had been scheduled originally for
the previous week, but that the commit
tee had been notified at the last minute
by the owners of the exhibition build
ing, where the courts wero laid out, that
the dates would have to be changed /;
that, in fact, the middle States officials
would have to accept March 80, 81 and
April or no dates at all.


AS for protesting Vincent Richards's
default, the facts show that Richards's
entry in the national event had been
only tentative; that his entry had been
accepted by telephone, which was con-
trary to the rules, and that the Seventh
Regiment Tennis Club therefore had no
right TO include him in the draw In the
first place.


Under the circumstances the national
executive committee will have no diff
Guilty in disposing Of the Seventh Regi-
ment Tennis Clubs protest. They need
but point out that the middle States
event could not have been held at any
other time than the three days finally
selected. and that the national title
tourney had every opportunity to attract
the tennis stars before the change in
the middle States date was announced.

In peril tonight. their ship. with her tail

Four men on the barge S. r. Mcdonald

Naval authorities here said at was
probable that the Arethusa, after she

the building was damaged, the chill

killed and fourteen captured by
Free State forces in the Fethard

Tipperary. Commandant Cooney
and Commandant Brennan were
among the prisoners.


The last of the English troops IN
Dublin began evacuating this after
noon. The barracks and the vice
regal lodge were turned over to the
Free State military authorities.


The Free State cabinet virtually
was completed this afternoon.
William T. Cosgrave will continue
as chief of the cabinet. Other Off
cials. whose tenure has been con-
verted from provisional to perma-
nent, were:


Gen. Richard Mulcahy, minister

agriculture, and J. J. Walsh. post
master general. Finian Lynch, for

sanitation and bathing utilities

THE curtain had fallen between acts


of brilliant revue in one of New


= York's most fashionable little thea
tres on upper Broadway. Out from the
wings tripped Miss Emma Haig, dainty
dancer whose nimble toes had carried her
far up the path of stage success. 1t was
a critical audience and little Miss Haig
aimed to please.


Her dance was supposed to symbolize
the seasons of the year. She had danced
lightly and gayly to represent Spring;
warmly and ardently to portray Summer;
now she was portraying the spirit OF
Autumn. To stress the richness and
beauty of the Fall season she had con-
ceived a graceful but vigorous leap and
high kick.


As the dance went on Miss Haig deter
mined to make this leap and kick even
more impressive than ever before. So she
with extraordinary vigor kicked straight
out and up with her left leg.


Now, theoretically-anda as it had hap
pened many times before-when the left
foot had arrived above her left ear and
far over her head, the impetus of the
kick should have raised her right toes off
the floor and Miss Haig should have gone
straight up into the air for two or three
feet. The impetus being spent, she should
have dropped lightly back


But that night something entirely diff
ferent happened. Instead of going
straight up the amazed little dancer found
herself sailing straight out over the foot
lights toward the audience!


In mid-passage there was tremendous

Upon the Unfortunate Clarinet
Players Head and How She
Caromed of 1t to the Rail
Dividing the Orchestra from the
Audience. Arrow Shows Where
Her Spine Was Broken by the Fall.
bump. Quickly there came another even
harder. And then little Miss Haig lapsed
into Inconsistencies.


Theatre employees carried her away. At
the same time, back in the audience,
others were carrying out an unconscious
clarinet player, whose head lolled rather
terrifyingly upon his shoulder.


What had happened was this: The ex-
traordinary force which the dancer had
put into her kick and leap had hurled her
forward like projectile, instead of send
ing her straight up like rocket.


In her swift flight over the orchestra
she had sat squarely upon the head of
Felippo Battista, clarinet player.


That unfortunate musician had passed
immediately in the middle of a sweet note
into sleep as profound as that which fol-
lows a punch on the jaw from Jack Demp-
sey! Her progress hardly checked by the
encounter, Miss Haig had caromed off
his head and had sat with stunning force
squarely upon the heavy rail that divides
the orchestra from the audience.


From there she had 'crumpled down at
the feet of the startled occupants of that
part of the first row.


Miss Haig had literally kicked herself
off the stage, and in doing so had broken
not only her back, but had dislocated and
almost broken the neck of the clarinet
player, who had been within her range!


So had come to pass an absolutely
unique accident, not only in Che history of
surgery, but Of the dance, the stage and
general gymnastics.


The doctor who had come out of the
audience examined both victims. A tele-
phone soon brought DR.. Philip CRAFTSMAN,
the same surgeon who had attended the
Follies star, Lillian Lorraine, last year
when she broke her neck. He ordered the
girl taken to an hospital. He lifted the
clarinet players chin in one hand and
placed the other hand at the back of his
neck a pressure, snarp oloW ~ tne
back of the neck Take him home," he
said. Though still unconscious, they did.


The accident which befell Emma Haig
occurred at the Music Box. Miss Haig
suffered what commonly has been be-
lieved to be an incurable injury. Her
back had been broken. She is one of
three beautiful young women who have
suffered the same injury and whose ex-
periences have been a valuable contribu-
ton to medical science. For, although
each had a broken back, one has entirely
recovered and the others are on the way
to recovery. They have driven forth the
bogie belief that a broken back cannot be
mended.

Periodic brake examinations. by car
owners themselves. is the cheapest
and easiest measure for avoiding ac-
cidents and keeping out of trouble
with the police. in the opinion of j.
W. Perry. general manager of the
automotive department of Johns
Manville. Inc. who outlined yester-
day dozen simple rules for keeping
brakes in good working order.


Adjust the brakes every thirty
days. maintaining between the brake
lining and the drum. all the way
around. clearance of about one
sixty-fourth of an inch.


Keep the right and left wheel brakes
operating with equal pressure. To
test this out. jack up the rear wheels.
start motor. and with car in high
gear. apply the brakes. Both wheels
should slow down uniformly.


Keep the brake lining clear of oil.
road grit and metal particles.


Clean the brake lining with kero-
sene once every two or three months.


Remove glazed spots on the brake
lining by roushening the surface with
a round or half-round file.


Tighten regularly all lock nuts and
rivets, TO avoid loosening the turn
buckles. and scoring the brake drums.


Keep the foot pedal and hand lever
in proper position. so that the foot
pedal will never go down far enough
to strike the floor board and so that
the hand lever will never pull back
and strike in its slot.


Test both brakes before starting.


Apply the brakes slowly.


Never let the tires slide.


Use the motor as a brake on hills.


Try out your brakes under various
conditions and see how quickly the
car will stop: then in service always
add liberal margin of safety.

BERLIN, July (By The Associated

June 10 during the Reichstag session.

paper writer, a member of the staff of
the Socialist newspaper "Vorwaerts,"
He belonged to the Left Wing OF the
Socialists and became prominently
identified with the Independent Social
list faction when the break came with
the majority party. He got into trouble
several times with the authorities dur
ing the troubles after the war in con-
nection with disturbances in Berlin
and elsewhere. but each time was ex-
onerated and set free.


Latterly Daumig appeared to have
lost favor with the wing of the parties
of the left most closely affiliated with
Moscow, although he had been one Of
the first leaders Of the pro- Moscow
faction.

girl on street who bobs her hair powders her
nose, paints her cheeks, smokes cigarettes, wears
short skirts, etc, is not above criticism. But she is
far advanced in the evolutionary process from her
unfortunate grandmama back in ancient Athens
She is human being with her own battles to wage
in the world. She has cut her hair short so she
can fight better. She has shortened her skirts
that she can move more swiftly She smokes
cigarettes because in the nerve-breaking atmos-
phere in which she lives, she needs stimulants
She paints her face and powders her nose because
she exposes these organs to the wind and the
sunshine.


The ancient Greek dame did none of these
things because she didn't have to. She her
husbands servant. She was very slightly removed
in fact, from the status of slavery Her condition
probably, was not enviable that of inmate
of Turkish harem at present. She never went
into the open air where the could burn her
nose Her lord and master wouldn't have permitted
it. Her dress and her habits were all characteristic
of slavery. They were pretty enough, it is true
But to be pretty was the Greek woman's one duty


Woman has fought for many centuries for the
right to get her nose sunburned, if she desires

sacred privilege for the sake of satisfying artists

progress that flow on forever toward the land of
promise

wheels by sticking their paint brushes between the
spokes.

LIMERICK, July 23 (Associated Press)
From the beginning to the end Of the
operations which ended with the cap
ture OF Limerick on Friday by the Free
State forces the rebels outnumbered the
Free State forces. Not more than zoo
Free State troops were engaged, whila
the rebel forces reached at least 1000.


The entire center OF the city was in
volved in the battle zone, the line of the
Free State troops extending the length
OF Thomas and Williams streets, and at
some points the conbatants were sepa-
rated by less than ten yards.


The fighting during the week con-
sisted mostly of rife and bombing duels.
Each side tunneed from house to house,
so that entire streets were transformed
into miniature fortresses. The rebels
from the outset occupied the strongest
positions. Their defeat was due to the
division of their forces by the isolation
of two important strongholds. the
Strand and Castle Barracks, by means
of an artillery assault and the threatened
encirclement of the rebels, who were
obliged to evacuate their positions to
avoid the cutting off On their retreat to
the south.


Before their evacuation the rebels set
fire to all the barracks by exploding
mines. and the flames spread with such
rapidly that 1t was useless to attempt
to subdue them. The new barracks. a
block of buildings erected around a
square of about 200 yards, were leveled
and Castle Barracks was destroyed, with
the exception of the thirteenth century
tower of King Johns Castle. One of the
two blocks comprising the ordnance bar
racks and the Frederick police barracks
also were destroyed.


Civilians Suffering.


The civilian population suffered acutely
during the fighting. Many were made
homeless and at times there was grave
menace of starvation. Famine was
averted by the Free state Gen. Brennan,
who supplied food to 10000 people. dis
tributing -four, bread. sugar and similar
necessaries, and operating the bakeries
under military control.


Nothing definite is known about the
leaders Of the rebels, except that Liam
Lynch, the so-called chief of staff, who
directed the operations In the early
stages returned to Clonmei The irreg-
ulars were well armed and had a large
supply of high explosives. They fed In
great haste at the end, destroying roads
and bridges.

BEACON, N Y, Aug. William

firemen and citizens. He killed Patrol

off the policeman's head with shot

narrowly missed policemen who VEN
tured near the house.


During the fighting Whites aged
mother was in the room with him.
Several citizens declare that they saw
her loading his pistols and shotgsns,
and others said that when the fire of
the policemen and firemen became
heavy and bullets began finding their
way into the room where White
crouched she placed her body between
the windows and her son and protected
him. She was not injured.


White himself was finally shot in
the head by James Devine. fireman
The wounded man staggered to the
hallway and pitched head first down
the stairs, mortally wounded At 9:30
o'clock tonight he died in the High
land Hospital.


Insane for seven Years.


White had been considered insane for
about seven years, but had never been
sent to an asylum and had not given any

trouble until to-day. The trouble began
when DIR. J. w. Jennings called on a
patient who lives next door TO the
White home. White made so much
noise. yelling and bowling. that the
physician went to the house and asked
him to be quiet. White became en-
ragged and hit the doctor with a chair.

could fire the physician escaped.

Patrolmen Lucy and Joseph Judge were
sent back to the house with him. Lucy
stepped across the threshold. White then
fired at Judge and the physician, but
missed and ran upstairs before the po
liceman could shoot. A crowd gath
cred. armed with stones, shotguns and
revolvers. and White barricaded thu
doors and shouted defiance from tbs
windows. He managed to keen down
below the window sill most OF the time
and althourh many shots were fired by
the crowd he wasn't hit. It was later
when the policemen and firemen and
State troopers came up. that his mother
shielded him with her body.


Firemcn Aid In Fight.


The Fire Department stretched three
lines OF hose and kept strong streams
of water playing against the windows.
but did not succeed in dislodging the
maniac. But while the troopers and
the police kept Whites attention with
volley of shots Chief of Police Moth
and Fireman Devine went to the Sec
ond story Of the house next door and
began shooting at White through a
window Almost the first shot from
Devine's gun took effect and White
staggered into the hall and fell down
the stairs.


When the police searched the house

Panels in three heavy oaken doors
were smashed and heavy locks shat
tered with sledge hammer welded
by general prohibition agents of
Zone Chief John ID. Appleby's division
yesterday afternoon when they raided
August Janssen's Hofbrau Hans, a res
taurant at 50 West Thirtieth Street.
extending through to Broadway.
Liquors, variously estimated to be
worth from $4,000 to $4,000, were
found behind the wrecked doors and
were confiscated. No choicer nor wider
assortment of ,lisuors ever have been
seized in raid, the agents said.


From 2:30 until o'clock the ten
agents engaged in the raid, all of
whom came here recently from various
parts of the country, carried out case
after case of the finest Scotch, Irish,
rye, bourbon and blended whiskies;
imported champagnes, absinthe, creme
de minthe and other cordials. These
were loaded in a truck from the
Knickerbocker warehouse and carted
away.


Proprietor Not Present


August Jansen, proprietor of the
place, was not present when the raiders
were working. He has home at Great
Neck, but was not reached there.
the seizure on the ground that all the
liquors had been purchased prior to
prohibition.


The agents charged the raid was
based on a purchase of beer at 40 cents
bottle made on the Jansen premises
several days ago by prohibition general
agents, and said that the date of the
purchase of the unusually fine stock of
wines and liquors did not enter into
the case.


When the raiders entered by the.
two entrances to the establishment all
tables in the restaurant on the first
crowded with fashionably dressed
women and men. The agents, who are
among the best trained in the govern
ment service, went about their work
Systematically and without disturbing
the diners.


The few agents who were forced to
walk through the dining room attracted
little attention. The army of employees
stood by silently while the agents
worked from the basement and engine
room up through the five floors, all of
which are occupied by the one concern.
Locked Door Smashed


On the fifth floor the agents came
upon heavy locked door, which en-
poyees said led to the linen closets.
They asked for key to this door and
said that no key was forthcoming. The
heavy hammer was brought into play
and three panels crashed from their
| frames. The agents reached through
| the apertures to work the lock from
| the inside. 1t refused to work, so it
was smashed.


| Inside the first door was hallway
into which two doors opened. These
were found locked. Employees pro-
tested that the doors shielded only a
valuable stock of linens. Keys were
asked for and when they did not arrive
in what the agents regarded as rea-
sonable time the hammer again began
| to swing. Panels We're torn out and
locks smashed Behind the doors the
alleged liquor stock was found nested
on shelves in orderly array.
| While the raid attracted little atten-
tion inside the restaurant it created
no end of curiosity on the streets when
the gayly painted warehouse van began
to bulge with its cargo of rare wines
and liquors.

In spite of the inclement weather.
between four and five thousand loval

started about o'clock and did not let
up until the close of the contest.

evident that there Would be much loose
playing. At regular intervals there
after Virginia lost much ground

Oppleman were forced to overcome with
their splendid line plunging. Prince
ton with fewer fumbles had the de-
clded advantage on the exchange of
punts. Vangerbig sending one forty
yard boot out of bounds only six inches
from the Virginia line. Arnod's re-
turn punts averaged about twenty-five
yards.


Princeton gained such advantages on
the punts that the ball was in Virginia
territory for almost the entire game,
although the Southerners did make
three earned first downs Whenever
the Tigers were near the opponents
they seemed powerless to advance, and
five times Smith was called upon to
drop kick, with the ball inside the 25-
yard line, but only once did he succeed
Princeton tried several forward passes,
but only one succeeded

attempting to punt, standing on the

basic lines of industry throughout the
country during April, according to the
monthly review Of general business and
financial conditions issued tonight by
the Federal Reserve Board

BILE in the metal industries. the board
declared. iron and steel becoming more

metals and other lines of industry,

panded operations.


In cotton textiles, however, the
month was much less encouraging, a
widespread strike in the New England
districts reducing mill activity, al
though in the Southern districts mills
generally continued to operate close
to capacity.

resulting from strikes, the board

fected to some extent the Improvement

cially the month showed the same ten

Sets up a troubled squawk

Above the trees


A swift and soaring hawk
His agitated parents


Rush homeward on the hop,
And shrilly shout
The warning out


That calls the Kingbird cop.
Upon a nearby locust


The foathered guardian swings,
With beady eyes
Upon the skies


And half extended wings;
And when. upon the signal,


He hurtles through the air
The bird of prey,
With scant delay,


Departs away from there.
The owl and jaybird tremble


To see that flying streak;
The eagles dread
That black-capped head


And needlc-Dointed beak.
And even Mr.. Tomcat


Lies fattencd on the ground
And for time
Renounces crime


When Kingbirds are around.
His size is not imposing,


He's gaunt and rather slight,
No bluebird's child
Appears more mild,


But how he loves to fight!

win turn in swift retreat

MOSCOW. January 5-Russia has

months of unspeakable horror before

summers crops may only slightly re-
lieve the gnawing famine.


At Tsaratsin. Saratoff. Samara. Ufa.
Orenburg and Kazan frozen bodies
are stacked high awaiting burial in
trenches which workmen cannot pre-
pare fast enough for the victims of
famine. exposure and typhus, and
every day the situation is growing
worse.


Toll May Reach 10000. 900.
American relief workers. who origi-
nally cautiously placed the number of
probable deaths in the famine area
this winter at 100000, now say that
100000 is low estimate. and many
say the number may reach 100000
or even more. This is possible par
ticularly since the shortage of horses,
to reach the more remote sections.
and since it is predicted the typhus
epidemic probably will be the worst
that Russia has ever suffered.


The Americans are feeding nearly
100000 children. and the British and
various other organizations are fur
nishing nournishment for at least
100. 900 under the most dangerous con-
ditions.

DR.. Reginald Farrar of the epidemics
commission of the league of nations
Miss Mary Paterson of the English

ner, of the German Red Cross have
died within the past week of typhus

Nancy Bobb and William Kenworthy

toff. and Anna Louise Strong of Phila-
delphia, who is associated with the
covering from the same malady in

relief administration, is convalescing
from the disease at Ufa.


These cases have occurred among
less than fifty foreign relief workers
in the famine area. who exerted every
precaution to avoid contracting
typhus. The disease is so prevalent
throughout all of the Volga region
and in Turkestan that the soviet gov
ernment has stopped all passenger
service to and from these regions.

George Newes of the British Save
the Children Fund reports he saw $50
frozen bodies, many of whom were
children, buried in trench at Sara
toff in one day. He says trainloads
of refugee children, underfed and
scantily clad, are riding from the
famine area in such pitiable con-
ditfon that the living children are
worse off than the dead.


The soviet government has agreed
to grant the American Relief Admin
istration the use of 5000 cars and 200
locomotives. required to move the
supplies which the $20,000.O00. just
appropriated by the United States,

The seventy mile an hour gale that
swept New York yesterday afternoon
tore the steamship Granite State, a
Shipping Board vessel. loose from her
moorings at West Thirtieth street.
She had no steam up and was not
under control. and she went plunging
up the Hudson River on the breast Of
the strongest tide that harbor and
river men have seen for many months


For two hours the big ship ran wild
veering gradually toward the New
Jersey shore and narrowly missing
collisions with the Hendrix Hudson
and other big. steamships. but finally
a dozen of the tugs that swarmed
about her managed to get lines aboard
the ship and stop her flight. She was
towed back to her anchorage and Sc
cured with two heavy anchors.


The current was against the vessel
when she started her run. but the tide
and wind combined proved much heavier
than the current. AS she veered and
twisted in the first gust Of wind after
her anchor lines broke the Granite State
caught up Stakeboat No. Of the Cor
nell Steamship Company and thereafter
carried the smaller craft along.

Mathewson. his wife and their ten-year-
old daughter. in danger all through the
excitement of having their boat crushed
against the sides of the Granite State
or being swept off by some of the other
ships that the runaway vessel ap-
preached.


The Granite state signaled for tugs
as soon as she began to drift up the
river. but she had got under such head
way by the time the first of them
reached her that they could do nothing.
Several got their lines aboard her. bur
they could not stop her. and were
whirlcd along in the wake of the big
ship.

ference for the first time when the
Turkish Strait commission meets.
Russian representatives will be ap-
pointed to this commission.


Tchitcherin conferred with Is
met Pasha, leader of the Turkish
delegation all day long. presenting
the Russian viewpoint and attempt
ing To stiffen the Turkish attitude

suasive powers to bear upon the

barred in the future to warships
Of all nations except Turkey.

decisive answer to the Russian

Nationalist Assembly at Angora.

bearing fresh instructions from
Angora for Ismet.

slams did not covet the Turkish
strait. He declared that Russia
was more interested in seeing that
the Turks got justice than anything
else"


Soviet Russia holds the view

they wish along the Dardanelles so
long as they allow free passage of
merchant ships of all nations" said
Tchitcherin.


When the conference enters its
third week tomorrow it will find an
unbroken deadlock on all questions.
The greatest resentment yet dis
played by the Turks was shown
over the allied proposals that the
capitulations be maintained at Con-
siantinople under the new treaty.
FIGHT CAPITUI.ATIONS.

said thar they could never permit
this. They declared they were un-

Il IL understood that the movement

than 1.00O. 900 Turkish and Greek
residents OF Greece. Thrace. and
Asia Minor. This question likewise
n in the hands of sub-commission.

will rage over future control Of the
Turkish Strait. Ii the Allies are

all nations without any fortifica-

To THE New YORK HERALD: Before
the advent of the tractor the American
farmer was handicapped in production
mule and the small capacity of the
horse drawn farm implements. The up
to date tractor with its enormous draw
bar power is particularly adapted to the
long bouts on the large prairie farms
of the middle West and of the North
west. One man driving tractor can
do as much plowing, cultivating or seed
ing as half dozen men formerly could
do driving horses.


The tractor calls for money running
into the thousands for the original
equipment and for much cash for gas,
oil and repairs while working. The
horse produces his own corn, oats and
hay and reproduces himself.


The tractor by displacng the horse
has closed one of the home markets for
the farmers, who sold their corn, oats
and hay to feed the horse and saved
transportation to the markets. The
acreage formerly used to produce food
for the horse is now free to create food
for man.


1t therefore follows that the tractor
has enormously increased the acreage
planting and the production of the
farmers. With our vast fertile and pro-
ductive prairies, power machinery put
into the hands of the many unguided
individual farmers will shortly fill all
markets with such an enormous guam
tity of all food products that the same
cannot be sold at the railroad stations
near to the farms at any price, how
ever small. and a complete stagnation
Of the farm industry. except in certain
sections near cities, will result.


Shall the American agriculturlst. the
farmer Of enterprise. the producer OF
quality and Of quantity be ruined and
eliminated by excess production brought
about by too much acreage planting
through lack of intelligent guidance?


VIII our Congress wait until the
whole farm industry is bankrupt before
giving intelligent advice to the Ameri-
can farmer? EDWIN McKNrGHr.

some time. Each member involved

James M. Force lived contentedly

ten miles distant from the Cogswell
abode.


Wives of the two men were Oft.
times seen together on the streets

home.

treatment. He was accompanied by

husband had agreed TO the plan.

cence, in which Forces wife and
Mrs. Cogswell took turns in nursing
him back to health, the trio jour
neyed back to Kansas City. Cogs-
well joined them there and a happy
reunion was staged.


The couples then returned to their
respective homes. Force left home
shortly after, ostensibly for short
fishing trip. Mrs. Cogswell left town
the same day, on her way, she said.
Ito Texas" Two divorce petitions

Boston is such sensitive creature
that it is difficult to rate accurately
the gravity of Miss Isadora Duncan's
high crimes and misdemeanors at
Symphony Hall. Apparently there
were many averted gazes when she
first appeared in full costume; and
later, when feeling the call Of Rus
!sia, she seized upon q piece of her
Grecian drapery and waved it above
her head, there were only few
horror stricken eyes bold enough to
observe the facts.


Was the drapery waved red? And
did Miss Duncan cry aloud that she
was Red? Plainly, when the clas-
sic atmosphere of Symphony Hall
was thus throbbing with wild and
appalling sights and sounds, accu-
rate testimony was difficult to find.
1t may have been green drapery that
wns snatched from it's accustomed
task, and Miss Duncan may have
merely remarked that she thought
well Of the Irish Republic. With
every sensibility on edge, her Puri-
tanical conscience throbbing pain
fully, her spectacles awry. how could
Boston possibly be sure what hap
pened!


Under the circumstances Mayor
Curley took the only sensible and
humane course He banished Miss
Duncan from Boston for all time.
Thus she escapes being jailed for
life, or some similar melancholy end.
and takes her place with the Mac
Monnies "Bacchante" and all the
other parts of Boston that have found
it necessary to live in New York for
their own and Boaton's good. Our
city has gained much through the
years by virtue Of that westbound 5
o'clock express. 1t runs little more

eyes dilating, she halted.

threshold. The haring candle

oughfares.

partment and the fuel administrn

coal famine. They feared that con
tinued cold weather would lead tc

licenses and i per cent on Soviet
government undertakings.

carefully guarded since the Soviets
began the new economic policy early
in 1921, but Leo Kameneff just q
year ago prophesied its early abolition
British official sources regard the new
move as defeat for Leonid Krassin,
SOVIET Minister of Trade, who has
held out for state control of foreign
commerce.

In the good, old days before the
direct primaries, when candidates
for the Senate were nominated by
the State Legislatures and for the
House by district convention, the
Herald declares that the Presidents
and party leaders were able to con-
troll their majorities in both Houses.


Undoubtedly, they were able to
control their majorities in both

Then, indeed, the railroads and

the selection of Senators and Repre-
sentatives. In those good, old days
before the direct primaries the

in the Senate and in the House
when he was doing the bidding of
some reactionary interests.


The real government was the in
visible government, first the power
full lobbies and behind them the
bankers and the financial interests
generally.


What pity it is that the direct
primaries have compelled repre-
sentatives to represent their con-
stituents. In New York State the
Republican party under Governor
Miller abolished direct primaries.
Now all the Progressives in the
Republican party want direct pri-
maries restored to restore the public
confidence in the party.

some and told with charming grace
book which should not be overlooked.

DRAZIL, greatest of Latin-American repub-
ID lies, will celebrate the centennial of her
independence the seventh of September. The
United States shows every disposition to help in
the observance. 1t will be, without doubt, gala
day IN the history of the republican idea.


The South American nation has the most
brilliant prospects, perhaps, of all world states.
She has wealth of natural resources which has
barely been tapped. She has progressive patriotic
government. She has intelligent citizenry. The
strides made by Brazil during the past few years
have been most remarkable. Great cities have
sprung up. Mile after mile of jungle has been
transformed into fertile fields. Her educational
system has been revolutonized Her people have
attained increased prosperity. II the same prog
ress continues Or another century the nation is
bound to be one of the four or FIVE premier powers
of the world


There is too great a tendency often feel,
for Americans to depreciate the prospects of Latin
American nations. There is too great inclna-
ton to underestimate the marvellous development
which has taken place during the past century.
The South American people have subdued nature
in peculiar continent. They have been obliged to
fight against semtropica conditions everywhere.
They have coped with many difficulties which
were unknown to American pioneers


Much of Brazil of course, still is jungle
almost impenetrable jungle In some parts Of this
great earthquakes in extent only than the United
States, Great Britain, Russia and China-white
men never have ventured But year after year
agriculture is pushed further and further into the
tropical tangle. Year after year towns spring
up further in the interior.


The cities of Brazil rank with the most beau
tful and the most progressive in the world. They
are wonder spots under the Southern Cross TJav-
elers marvel at them. From them many cities of
the United States learn valuable lessons.


Brazil offers substantial hope for the poverty
stricken Of the world. Wonderful oppor-
tunities always exist wherever there is undevel-
oped land This the southern republic has to offer
What she most needs is men and more men
intelligent, hard-working, ambitious men. She
needs the thrifty peasants of crowded Europe
with their inherited culture and their determine
tion to rise in the world She needs to become a
melting pot for the excellent stocks of the Cau-
easian race-for the Russian people, the Balkan
people the Italian people, the Austrian people and
the rest.


The nation has had a picturesque and compli-
mentary history Alone of new world nations she
supported monarchy for time after the shackles
of European royalty had been cast off But her
people were essentially republican in ideals The
example of Brazil proved conclusively that there
place for hereditary thrones in the new
world. The people of the Western hemisphere are
not constituted that they can kow-tow to
crowned heads for long. Brazirs great develop.
ment has been under the republican form of gov
ernment. 1t will continue under the same form
of government


She starts her second century of independent
life with prospects of which all other nations may
we'll be jealous.

HUNTINGTON, L. l., Nov. 27.-John
J. Leitch was shot and killed by Edgar
Scudder here tonight after Leitch had
shot and seriously wounded his former
fancee, seventeen-year-old Rose Land
RISER, upon whom he had called at
Scudder's home, ostensibly for the pur-
pose of getting back his engagement
ring.


Leitch was twenty-nine years old and
lived in Northport. He and Miss Sand
risser had been engaged for some time.
The engagement was broken off yes
terday. When they returned from
their customary Sunday motor trip, the
girl flung herself into the arms of Mrs.
tScudder, with whom she has been stay
ing because Of quarrel with her
family, and told her that she never
could marry Leitch and he was to call
this evening for his ring.


His Demeanor unchanged


He called soon after supper and
neither Mr.. Scudder nor his wife no.
ticed anything unusual in his de-
meanor. AS was their custom when
he came to see their guest, they retired
TO the kitchen, leaving the living room
to Leitch and Miss Sandrisser.


The two had been sitting there only
short time when the Scudders heard
a shot. They ran into the living room,
Mrs. Scudder ahead of her husband.
She was almost upset by Leitch, who
was rushing from the room, in which
his former fiancee lay senseless on the
floor, bullet through her head.


Leitch, she says, leveled his revolver
at her and pulled the trigger. Mrs.
Scudder was so close to him that she
DETECTED the barrel with quick mo-
tion of her arm and the bullet sped
past her and buried itself in the wall.


Fires Over Fugitive's Head


By this time Scudder was in the
room, his shotgun in his hand, both
barrels loaded and cooked. Leitch was
disappearing through the door. Scud-
der followed him. Leitch jumped into
his automobile and Scudder fired one
barrel. He aimed over Leitch's head,
he said, and intended merely to scare
him away.


Instead of speeding away, Scudder
says, Leitch began to circle the drive
way in front of the house, and Scudder,
seeing him returning toward him, fired
the second barrel. The charge struck
Leitch in the heart and he fell over
the steering wheel, while his car
brought up against tree.


Deputy Sheriff Wanzell was notified
and took Scudder to his Office, though
not under arrest, to await the arrival
of DR. Edward S. Moore, Coroner.

great portion OF the country. Meteor
logically speaking. the winds and the
barometric pressures are acting contrary
to nature. The air is sluggish and there
is little movement in high or low strata,

cannot journey over the country.


With the exception of California and

the east Gulf coast, few areas have had

Below Zero and No shelter.

British spies learned of his whereabouts and the

A weakening Influence in the money
market last week was the shortage of
credit. Banks will advance money only
to their most substantial customers. SO
that they can keep their factories going.
There are several instances where firms
with orders ahead could not raise the
money to pay their workers. One glove
factory which had sold It's entire output
to England could not raise the three
months necessary credit to make its
winter deliveries.


A big industry with large stock OF
raw materials on hand. as, for example.
the Siemens n Schuckert firm. with a
large supply of copper, can obtain credit
at home and abroad. But foreign and
domestic credits are becoming almost
prohibitively costly. The result is that
factories are reducing their output and
personnel in order to keep within their
credit limit Because of the depreciation
in the mark most firms now need several
times as much credit for their daily rum
ming expenses as their total original
capitalization.


Firms supplying the domestic mar
ket also are reducing their output owing
to the deprecated buying power or the
German people. This reduction Is most
marked in food, linen and household
goods manufacturers. A leading whole
sale merchant told THE NEW YORK
HERALD correspondent that while his
sales in volume amount to about 20 per
cent. of the pre-war volume, reck-
oned In dollars they amount to about
so per cent. of before the war receipts.
Foreigners are buying 60 per cent. OF
his wares. he said, and while his paper
mark turnover seems fabulous turn
over with each slump in the mark
the real dollar turnover decreases.

CHICAGO. August 19.-With the
temperature in Chicago lowering
around IS degrees yesterday. the local
weather bureau announced that the
heat wave. which has held the city
in its grip for the last two days. has
been broken. Ten persons died here
as result of the heat.


CLEVELAND, Ohio, August 10
Thunderstorms late yesterday brought
relief from the heat wave which
struck Ohio several days ago, but not
until three persons had dropped dead.


COLUMBUS. Ohio. August 19.-Heat
yesterday caused the death of one
person and prostration of another.
Maximum official temperature was
93.2. which is within one-tenth of
degree Of the years record. Heavy
rain, accompanied by much lightning
last night. brought relief. Practi-
cally all electric lights in the city
were put out of commission for al
most an hour, and trolley cars idled
on their tracks.

land Medical Department, northeast

flames.

With them the aims and purposes of
scout work, emphasizing the tend
ency H. has to counteract some of
the modern influences. which arc not
wholly beneficial to girls. The scouts
assembled at the hall and were photo
graphed with Mrs. Hoover. AT Mrs.
Hoover's request the girls recited
the scout laws, the promise, motto
and slogan, and sang "America' and
The Star Spangled Banner" after
which they all saluted the flag.

outdoor life and nature study long
before the Girl Scouts were organ
lied. When she went with her par
child that was good and useful was
spoken of as good scout" and she
expressed belief that this was the
origin of the term. In concluding
her talk. she invited the girls TO visit
her at her home in Washington at the
end of the season and make report on
their summers work.

Fengtien forces from the southern
front at Manchang and the northern
fighting area are pouring through
Tientsin toward ShunliangchenE.
from which their leader. Gen. Chang
Tso-Lin, is reported to have with
drawn, seeking to reorganize his
army.


Reports from Tientsin say the rail-
road yards there are choked with
troop trains damned with soldiers,
200 to each car. Following five train
loads last night 1t was estimated to-
day that 5000 men had passed
through. with 10000 more in the rail-
road yards.


The troops from the northern front
are disheartened. and say they have
been fighting for three days without
food at Fengtai and Langfang. They
are anxious to return to Mukden.


The men are still heavily armed. but
are maintaining discipline. showing no
tendency toward footing or disorder.
The Tientsin authorities, however, are
guarding the railroad yards. refusing
to permit the troops to leave the sta
ton. Bread is being distributed to the
soldiers. all of whom on their arrival
made wild rush. pleading for water.
A few have been wounded by the
guards. There has been no disorder,
but Tientsin is apprehensive.
American troops are guarding the
property of their nationals and keep
ing watch 1t the railway station. The
United States cruiser Huron arrived
yesterday and landed $50 marines. Re-
ports that the railroad line to Mukden
has been cut by the forces of Gen WI
Pei-Fu are unverified.


An American military observer re-
turning to Tientsin from Machang
says Changes forces are still holding
seven kilometers beyond that town,
where there is occasional firing He
saw scores of dead. while, hundreds of
wounded were uncared for in the i'm
provised, inadequate hospitals, where
they lay pleading for water and food.

Another link in the chain that is bringing Wash
ingon into closer touch with the people, business and
products of that portion of Virginia lying along the
Potomac, will be the operation of the steamer
MAJESTIC by company of Washington business
men familiar with the field which the steamer will
touch The steamer, now being fitted for its duties
will engage not only in freight but passenger service
and Its managers expect to make traffic arrange
ments with other steamship lines and with rail
roads The first trip will probably be about April l.


This new river service, together with trucks
operating between the Northern Neck of Virginia
and Washington ought to aid materially in develop
ing most satisfactory trade relations between Wash
ington and desirable portion of the mother State
of the nation. The prospects all the brighter
because the stockholders of the new company are
acquainted with the people and the needs of the
territory to be served and believe that Washington
is the logical city to supply this territory and to
use the products to be brought from it.


The policy will be to put freight rates the
lowest possible basis an encouragement to Vir-
ginians to ship their products here and to Wash
ingonians to sell to their neghbors along the lower
Potomac. Wholesale dealers of this city have
promised to send statesmen into the new territory,
and retail houses will not fail to look out for their
interests by offering attractive bargains to the Vir
ginians who will turn this way for their shopping


Water transportation between Washington and
Potomac river ports has been greatly restricted since
the war-to the detriment of this city. Baltimore
business men have been alert, though and have left
nothing undone to divert this river business to that
city.


The Baltimore Chamber of Commerce some time
ago arose masse in protest against the threat OF
the Pennsylvania railroad to remove their bay and
river service. It would have meant the loss Of
hundreds of thousands of dollars each year to that
city.


All the people of Washington will benefit by sup
porting every movement that means quick and
friendly touch with Virginia and Maryland territory
which has heretofore felt itself dependent Balti-
more in business dealings The steamers and trucks

NVER 400 midshipmen who graduated from
~ the United States Naval Academy at An
napolis yesterday enter the profession of with
misgivings.


The sunny horizons which have stretched be-
fore former graduates are couded for these young
men, The calling of John Paul Jones, of Law
renee, of Perry, of Farragut and of Dewey does
not hold forth the same promises as it did few
years ago. The disarmament conference at Wash
ington reached agreements which bode III for the
future of warfare on the high seas.


1t is possible that none of these young off
GERS ever will direct single shot against hostile
ship. 1t is not improbable that they will win
fame through herosm and skill in battle.


But they have no reason to feel that their edu-
cation has been in vain. They have been given not
only general but highly technical education.
They should have better opportunities in the world
than graduates of most other colleges this year.
The Annapolis men have, at least, enough prac-
tca knowledge and understanding to earn living
in the varied industrial field of their country. They
have been trained not only mentally but physically.
They know mathematics and they endure the
hard life necessary for advancement in almost any
line.


Experts in navigation woefully lacking in the
United States. Outside the navy there have been
few college-trained men on the high For over
a half century America has not been seafaring
nation. Its development has been inland. Its best
genius has gone for the upbuildng Of factories and
the settlement of prairies. But the time has come
when the must turn to the again. For
eign trade is becoming of greater and greater i'm
portance The fact that all the countrys exports
must be carried in foreign bottoms is encourag-
ing. Until recently this has been the for all
practical purposes.


Annapolis graduates rest easy they look
to the future. They have the training needed to
lead in the field, to emulate the New Eng
landers of old, who carried the stars and stripes
into all the ports OF the world.


Perhaps the young officers will have even
better opportunities if circumstances rob them Of
careers in the navy. Outside the service men often
lead harder lives, but win greater rewards. But
yet it is by means certain that their services
not needed in fighting. Disarmament has
not yet come. There is certainty that the days
of ocean battles are over. The midshipmen have
fine prospects, whatever results may in the
next few years from the almost universal senti-
ment against expensive and war-provokng fleets.

cifuliy put out his misery when the
enemy came 10 seize him.

des Fetes recently. Some have gallant

dren from drowning. stopped runaway
horses, caught burglars, protected sheep
and stood silent guard over their mas
ters' lives and homes. Three OF them

The German government last

Hitler had planned to move the

Cancelled.

Interior Schweyer, who informed

the national government and that
the Bavarian. government could not
interfere with the orders from Ber'
lin.

saturday would find them masters

cheers.

All the nationalist groups In Ba-
varia have now united in a League

The republican senators are plead
ing for an early vote on the tariff.
They see the danger of delay. They
want as much time as possible for the
new measure to show" the country
before election day. They are warned
by bits of tariff history.


Thirty-two years ago the Mckinley
tariff revision. after stormy passage
through Congress. particularly through
the Senate, went into operation only
few weeks before election day, with
the result that the vote was taken
while the congressional clamor was
still fresh in memory. The new law
was condemned at the polls largely on
the strength of what its enemies had
said about it on Capitol Hill.


Twenty-eight years ago the German
Wilson tariff revision. after stormy
passage through Congress. and the
narrowest escape from shipwreck in
the Senate, went into operation only
a few months before election day, and
without President Clevelands sigma
ture, with the result that the demo-
cratic party, which was responsible for
the measure, lost the election. The re-
publicans had almost a walkaway, and
two years later won both Congress and
the presidency.


Election day is only six months
away. and what is called the Fordney
bill has just entered the Senate whirl-
pool. How soon, and in what shape,
will it emerge? Or will 1t emerge in
any shape before the voters gather to
determine the complexion of the Sixty
eighth Congress? The republican anX-
iety is we'll justified. The situation is
ticklish.

An X-ray apparatus gives off
rays of varying penetrative power.
These rays which penetrate but
slightly are called soft rays, and
those that penetrate deeply are
known as hard rays. The soft
rays are the most abundant and
likely to damage the skin, so they
have to be filtered out. This is
done by interposing' a substance
between the X-iay tube and the
patient through which the hard
rays will pass and exert their
beneficent effects but which win
bar effectually the passage of any
soft rays. Leather was once used
for this purpose, and finally zinc
and copper filters were employed.


American workers have concen-
trated more upon the study of
radium, and now it seems that
the combined knowledge of the
two types of experts will bring
about very remarkable results in
behalf of suffering humanity.

YOSEMITE, Cal. March 12.--Successful

been accomplished. After several weeks
of experiment results are so satisfactory
that announcement has been authorized
that wireless henceforth will be per-
manent method of communication with
the popular resort, though it may not be
open for commercial use until next win-
ter.


Edwin j. Symnnes of Alameda put in
the first wireless set for his own amuse-
ment and has received messages from
several score damped and undamped
wave stations. including Honolulu and
Catalina Island. Government authori-
ties also have put in a station, which
will be used to keep in touch with the
outside world when State wide storms
interfere with wire communication and
in touch with Glacier Point. now open
TO visitors throughout the year, which
is 3,25i feet sheer above Yosemite Val
ley.


Because Yosemite Valley is literally
hole in the ground" some wireless ex-
perts declared local conditions were en-
tireiy against successful operation of a
wireless station here. Yosemite's granite
cliffs rise straight into the air for 3,400,
1000 and occasionally 5000 feet. Never
theless valley folk recently have been
getting news reports, weather predic-
tions, market quotations and lots of
good music right out Of the air. with no
other aerial than wires strung between
two of the giant trees with which the

MISS MARIE EHLERs was. shopping

Hurriedly paying for her purchases she
went out to see what was going on.


1t was political parade and the uproar

of the procession. A score of earnest
colored musicians were putting away at
their horns and creating weird combina-

Along with thousands of other specta-
tors Miss Ehlers smiled-and then she
felt twitch in her shoulder. Her other
shoulder jerked upward without any
warning. Her left hip shook violently.
There was an answering convulsive move
ment of her right hip, and then her
shoulders and hips began jerking in all
directions at once!


She was doing an involuntary and very
public "shimmy'' and was utterly power
less to stand still


The scores of spectators of the pa
rade were quick to notice Miss Ehlers's
strange conduct and formed ring about
the unfortunate girl, who shivered and
shimmyed and shook faster and faster as
the musicians increased the cadence of
the rag-time melody.


Her purchases fell from under her arm.
Her hat worked down over her eyes. Her
handbag jiggled up and down with the
movement of her shoulders, and there was
nothing she could do to prevent it!


Worst of all, the laughing spectators
of her humiliation were quite sure that
she was staging an open-air dance for
their benefit and applauded with all their
might apd main.


A policeman noticed the commotion and
rode up to the curbing on which the un-
happy Miss Ehlers stood-and shook.
Jumping from his horse, he waded into
the crowd and seized her arm.


Here! none of that" he said. where
do you think you are? In Egypt?"

violently than ever. And then the police
man saw from the intense surprise and
embarrassment that was pictured upon
